speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question of privilege which I should like to put briefly before the house, which affects all members of the house and the rights of parliament. It is with regard to a press release, small as it may be, in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald for Friday, July 10, 1964, page 19, which reads as follows:
Award of a $18,616 public works department contract to Colin R. MacDonald Limited of Antigonish for repairs to pier A at Pictou was announced from the office of labour minister Allan J. Mac-Eachen here yesterday.
On July 3 I placed a question on the order paper, being question No. 1,423, which asked the number of tenderers and the amounts of the various tenders for harbour improvements and repairs to pier A at Pictou, and I also asked to whom the contract would be awarded. On checking Hansard it will be seen that this question was not answered. What has been done by the minister is to circumvent the rights of parliament. The order paper today is even more sacred following the changes in the rules, and although the minister may have been in Switzerland or perhaps visiting the Queen to right the wrongs of the Minister of Transport in the United Kingdom, this is not the first time this has come before parliament and the rights of parliament must be upheld. I think the government must take due notice of this.

subsubtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
I wish to table, as I told the hon. member for Greenwood I would, the memorandum of the government of the Soviet union regarding certain proposals to strengthen the effectiveness of the United Nations in safeguarding international peace and security. I am tabling copies in French and in English.
On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: In connection with matters arising out of the tabling of the document referred to a few moments ago by the Acting Prime Minister, I would ask him whether the apparent change of attitude on the part of the Soviet union in connection with peace keeping operations has been followed up by any action by the U.S.S.R. to place itself in a position of responsibility in the United Nations by arranging to pay its membership dues and its share of expenses in connection with peace keeping. Would the minister say whether there has been any consultation with the Soviet union in this regard, and does this recent action on the part of that country indicate that an arrangement has been made whereby the voting rights of the U.S.S.R. which would end in September through failure to pay arrears are not now likely to be affected?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: There has been no change, since the distribution of this proposal by the Soviet union for a permanent United Nations peace force, in the amount of money which the international court of justice, by way an advisory opinion, has said is owing by the Soviet union to the United Nations. There have been some discussions with the Soviet union with regard to the confrontation that will inevitably face that country at the next general assembly under article 19 of the charter, if some moneys have not been paid by the Soviet union to reduce its total indebtedness to a figure less than the assessment owing by the Soviet union to the United Nations for the previous two years. The secretary general himself is leaving tonight on a tour that will take him to a number of countries, including the Soviet union. I do not know what will be the nature of their discussions, but I would be surprised if this were not one of the subjects to be discussed at that time.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
I thank the minister for his very full answer, and ask him this question. Have any representations been made by Canada directly to the U.S.S.R. pressing upon that country and other countries that are in default the necessity of respecting their undertakings and responsibilities under the charter, and in particular the payment of their share which, as the minister has

Wheat Sales to Poland stated, was declared to be a proper levy in an advisory judgment of the world court?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, there have been at least two occasions when I, on behalf of the government of Canada, have discussed this matter with spokesmen of that government.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of the fact that the proposal of the Soviet union regarding peace keeping operations has now been received by the government of Canada, could I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs what reply the Canadian government intends to give, whether it is favourably disposed to the proposal and whether in the minister's opinion this proposal would place peace keeping forces entirely under the jurisdiction of the security council and reduce the powers enjoyed by the assembly.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL RESPECTING PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the proposal of the Soviet union is not addressed to any country. It was generally distributed this morning to all delegations at the United Nations. I have already indicated in the external affairs committee last week some of my reactions to the proposal. I would simply say now that if it represents, as the right hon. gentleman suggested we should hope it might, a positive attempt on the part of the Soviet union to share in all the obligations having to do with United Nations peace keeping responsibilities, then it is certainly to be welcomed. It is in a spirit of constructive interpretation that Canada is examining this proposal.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: WHEAT-ANNOUNCEMENT OP FURTHER SALE TO POLAND
speechtext:
The Canadian wheat board is announcing in Winnipeg today that it has negotiated a contract for the sale of approximately 200,000 metric tons of wheat for shipment to Poland. This sale, totalling about 7.4 million bushels, is for shipment during the period August to November, 1964. This is the second sale made to Poland under the provisions of the long term agreement signed on November 5, 1963 and completes the quantities Poland had agreed to buy during the first year of the three year agreement.
Payment for the wheat is to be made on the basis of 10 per cent at time of shipment

with the remaining balance to be paid in equal instalments plus interest at two, two and a half and three years respectively. These credit arrangements were authorized by the government of Canada under the provisions of the Export Credits Insurance Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. Waller L. Gordon (Minisler of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-110, to facilitate the making of loans to students.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with considerable satisfaction that the government has placed before the house this legislation to launch the Canada student loans plan. From references already made to this subject in various quarters I know that, whatever may be said of the details, the purposes and principles of this bill command widespread support.
This is surely as it should be. It is a cliche to say that a country's future depends upon its young people. But cliches are often true, and the importance of the truth embodied in this one can scarcely be overstated. The need for financial assistance, such as the loan plan that we are now considering, can be established in economic terms, in statistical terms and, most important, in terms of human lives and human hopes.
In economic terms, Canada's future strength and prosperity depend not only on the quality of our natural resources, about which we so often remind ourselves, lout even more on the quality of our human resources. This is particularly true if we are determined, as indeed we are, to be more than hewers of wood and drawers of water. We must make sure, in the complex and competitive world of today, that an ever growing proportion of our young men and women have ready access to the benefits of higher education. In this age where undereducation so often spells underemployment, we must put forward very special efforts to ensure that no competent student lacks the financial support to continue his education beyond high school.
In statistical terms the need for new and very substantial financial facilities is easy to demonstrate. As is well known, we are in the early stages of an unprecedented "bulge" in our population at the university entrance age. This results from an unprecedented rise in the Canadian birth rate in the late war and post-war years. Statistical estimates published by the Canadian universities foundation suggest that rates of increase in university attendance during the rest of this decade could exceed 10 per cent per year. As hon. members know, the government has recognized the need for the provinces to have a


greater share of revenues and higher equalization grants to meet such educational requirements.
This growth in the number of students in itself would greatly overstrain existing arrangements for student financing. In addition, however, one must take into account that because these war babies and post-war babies were spaced unusually close together, families will now be faced with the cost of keeping not one but possibly two or three of their children in college at the same time. This will accentuate the need for financial support.
Moreover, because the population of posthigh school age is and will continue to be unusually large, students will experience unusual difficulty in finding summer jobs. Actually the number of summer jobs will no doubt be increasing, but the increase of students may be expected to exceed them. This again constitutes a special need for setting up enlarged arrangements for student financing at this time.
Finally, and most importantly, the need, the great and growing need, exists not merely as an economic problem or as a statistical projection, but as a pressing problem for the young men and women of this country. It exists for them and it exists for their families, the older families that they grew up with and the younger families they are even now founding and forming. A university education or its vocational equivalent is the highest achievement of our educational system, and it should be within the financial grasp of every young Canadian who is capable of making good use of it.
There was a time when some people actually believe that the children of the well to do, those who could afford to buy a university education, were the only ones who should be entitled to profit from it, and that people in poorer circumstances should not aspire to it.
This belief has long since been proven false. If we do not provide the means whereby all children with the necessary abilities can share the privilege of higher education, we are doing them a grave injustice and we are denying to our country a source of economic and intellectual benefit which we can ill afford to sacrifice.
Higher education is an investment, an investment for the individual and an investment for the society in which he lives. Both will be the richer as a result. The student's earning power may be expected to increase

substantially on the basis of such an investment. This is why it makes sense tor him, and for his government, that he should borrow in order to make this investment. It also makes sense for the individual and his government to share the cost of this investment, and this is exactly what the Canada student loans plan sets out to do. In the early stages, while the student is not yet earning, the government bears the whole cost. Later, when the student has graduated and has had some time to settle down and start earning, he himself takes over the debt. But still the government stands behind him, guaranteeing his loan, moderating its cost to him and taking over in case of his death.
What, in practical terms, can the Canada student loan plan offer to a young student? It can offer him annual loans up to $1,000 a year and total loans up to $5,000. The actual amount and terms of the loans to any individual will, of course, be related to his individual requirements and prospective earning capacity. For example, a student living in a university residence or in a boarding house may well need more than a student living at home. Again, a student in a course such as medicine, which is very expensive, may require more than a student in nursing. Obviously the prospective doctor can afford to take on a larger debt than the prospective nurse.
To be eligible for a loan a student must have attained a satisfactory scholastic standard-a judgment that is naturally to be made, under our plan, by the educational authorities. He must also, as is required in other student loan plans and as is essential to prevent possible abuse and to protect the taxpayer, make it clear to the authorities that he actually needs the loan. Given eligibility on these grounds, a student will qualify for a loan if he is a Canadian citizen or if he has resided in Canada for at least a year and intends to continue to reside here.
The loans are to be made to full time students. One of the main purposes of this plan is to make it possible for students whose university education would otherwise drag on over many years of part time work or night courses to complete their college education more quickly and to reap its intellectual and financial benefits at an earlier age.
Students who are residents of other countries will not be eligible for loans under the Canada student loans plan. Students from the richer countries abroad who choose to study here will have their own sources of finance; with our universities already crowded we do 20220-345

not consider we should offer them special inducements to come here. Students from the less developed countries may, of course, obtain educational assistance under several Canadian programs.
Apart from this, both undergraduate and graduate students may qualify under our plan. Moreover, as I have already implied, it will not be limited to students proceeding to an academic degree. It can cover any form of post-secondary school education. In order to designate the institutions which qualify in this category, bearing in mind the differences across Canada in this regard, we have invited the help of the provincial governments. They, or authorities designated by them, are to specify the institutions which student borrowers may attend, whether at home or abroad. It is clear from our discussions with provincial representatives that the coverage will be as comprehensive as reasonable administrative and educational standards can permit.
In this connection it is relevant to record that all the provinces, with but one exception, already operate some sort of general student loan plan. In virtually every case the amounts which can be made available for the loan plan, and in some cases to individual students, are substantially less than are to be made available under the Canada student loans plan. Nevertheless we are anxious both to learn from their experience and, if they are agreeable, to make use of their administrative machinery including the machinery set up for establishing student eligibility.
We recognize that the provinces are better able than the federal government to determine which students require assistance for the pursuit of their education in provincial educational institutions. Consequently we are hopeful that provincial governments will be prepared to act as partners in the Canada student loans plan through making available their machinery for establishing the eligibility of students for loans. Not only would this simplify the administration of the Canada student loans plan-it would be very difficult for the federal government itself to duplicate provincial machinery-but it would also serve as a useful point of liaison between the actual educational institutions, which clearly fall in the provincial jurisdiction, and a plan for guaranteed bank loans to students provided by the federal government.
Accordingly it is our expectation that students seeking loans under the Canada plan will, in each province, file applications through familiar and established channels. I expect that in almost every case a student will file his

Loans to Students
application in the province where he lives, but in certain cases where he pursues his studies in another province it may transpire that his application should be filed there.
I should emphasize that it is not our purpose to supersede any existing plan or arrangement. Some may well be modified, a few may possibly be discontinued; but in the field of student assistance there is room for many and diverse arrangements. A big national plan can carry the main financial problem, but other bodies can allow themselves greater flexibility, greater adaptability to local conditions and personal needs of students.
In this respect I would like to pay tribute particularly to the existing provincial plans and university plans, and to private plans such as those of the chartered banks themselves and such imaginative and worth-while arrangements as the Canadian scholarship trust plan which was initiated a few years ago.
Once a student has received from the appropriate provincially designated educational body or its agent-perhaps a student loan board; perhaps a university or governmental body in the province where he resides-a certificate for a loan of a specified amount, he or she will go to a bank to arrange the loan. The student can go to any branch of any chartered bank, either near his home or near his university. While the banker is not under compulsion to make the loan-after all, he is lending the money that other people have deposited with him-it would only be in exceptional cases that he would find a reason to question the amount stated on the certificate. He will, of course, satisfy himself that the person who presents a Canada student loan plan certificate is indeed the student to whom it has been issued, but as long as there is no corner cutting or double dealing-and I am sure there will be none of this-the student may normally expect to get his loan.
The loan he obtains, however, will differ in very important respects from the loans the same banker is making to other people. The student, under the Canada plan, will be specially favoured in three ways. First, he will not have to pay any interest on his loan or repay any part of the capital until six months after he has completed his studies. In the meanwhile the government will pay the interest to the bank. Second, when the time comes for the student to begin to pay interest and repay his loan it will cost him less than an ordinary borrower who, on a

personal loan, will normally pay his banker the maximum legal rate of 6 per cent and a service charge as well. Under the Canada plan the government which guarantees the loan will also establish from time to time the maximum interest rate that may be charged, and no additional service charges will be permissible.

1 per cent of the total loans outstanding. Under the student loan plan there will be an additional cost to the government during the interest free period enjoyed by each student borrower, but even making allowance for this the costs will be substantially less than would be involved in any other arrangement. The Canadian government has a natural advantage in sponsoring this sort of system on a large scale, country-wide basis.
I turn now from the plan as it will look to the student to the plan as it will look to parliament in its traditional role of custodian of the national purse and defender of the national taxpayer. At the outset let me reassert what is probably clear from what I have already said. The government has not approached this plan in any penny pinching spirit. We have been anxious to avoid waste and duplication in administration, but we are not proposing to parliament financial limits that are expected or intended to be restrictive. On the contrary, they are expected to accommodate all reasonable needs; and if, perchance, actual needs should outrun our expectations we shall bring the matter back to parliament for amendment. We can envisage that under the system we have in mind the outstanding loans at the end of five years could well be of the order of $200 million. At the end of 10 years we would expect them to be of the order of half a billion dollars.
For the first year of the plan, beginning this fall, we propose that parliament should provide for guaranteed bank loans up to $40 million. This, we calculate, would provide for a loan exceeding $500 for one out of every three students enrolled, a proportion that is unlikely to be reached in the first year of the plan or, indeed, for several years. This is the judgment of all the people whom we have consulted in this matter who have been administering loan plans for some years.
We also provide in the draft legislation for year by year escalation in the total to be guaranteed. Beginning from $40 million, this escalation is calculated on the basis of the growth of the age group in our population that may be expected to take advantage of university education and vocational training facilities. For calculation purposes, this group is 18 to 24 inclusive. Lest there be any misunderstanding, let me stress that this age group is used solely for purposes of statistical estimates. The benefits of the plan are available to students of any age, below 18 or above 24 or within those limits.
I might mention also the fact that the bill before the house establishes that bank loans

Loans to Students
under this legislation are to be recoverable even though they may be made to minors. While under normal circumstances a student who is not of full age may be expected to have his loan endorsed by a parent or someone else whose guarantee would be acceptable to a bank, we feel that this is not necessary, nor even desirable, if Canada provides a guarantee along the lines provided in this bill. We would expect that normally the parent would be aware of the application, but we would not wish to stipulate that the loan would require approval of the parent. To our way of thinking, it is better for all concerned that the student should take full responsibility and should feel fully responsible from the start.
Not only does the annual total grow from year to year on the basis of the 18 to 24 age group, it is also divided, year by year, among the provinces on the basis of the distribution across the country of the same age group. Thus the $40 million available in the first year would be divided approximately in the following amounts, using 1963 population data. Of the total of $40 million, $1.14 million would be allocated for Newfoundland; Prince Edward Island, $0.23 million; Nova Scotia, $1.73 million; New Brunswick, $1.37 million; Quebec, $12.96 million; Ontario, $12.49 million; Manitoba, $1.98 million; Saskatchewan, $1.89 million; Alberta, $2.89 million; British Columbia, $3.24 million; Yukon and Northwest Territories together, $0.08 million.
We considered the possibility of a system which was based not on provincial allocations but on some sort of uniform educational standard which would be equally applicable in any part or portion of the country. However, it soon became clear that such a uniform standard was impossible to devise and, even if it could be devised, would be impossible to apply. We are satisfied that the provincial allocation arrangement is more fair and more defensible than any alternative. Moreover, while different criteria could be considered both for the escalation and for the division between provinces, the use of the age group 18 to 24 appears to be at once the simplest and the most generally acceptable. I might add that if over the years serious anomalies show up the matter would be brought back to parliament for revision.
I have already explained that this plan, while very substantial in its proportions and in its provisions for future growth, is nevertheless quite economical from the point of view of the public purse. Actually, costs in the first year, even if all provinces used

all their quotas and the whole $40 million were used up, would not be likely to exceed $2 million. In later years, when the outstanding loans would accumulate and the interest burden therefore grow, and when the government was meeting its guarantees, the costs could rise appreciably. Nevertheless I believe they will always look reasonable and moderate by comparison with the size of the plan and the importance of its purpose.
When the Canadian student loan plan was discussed at the provincial conference in Quebec last March we made it clear that if a province decided to rely entirely on its own student loan plan instead of participating in the Canada plan, it would be able to receive equivalent compensation. The bill makes provision for this. As hon. members know, the province of Quebec has indicated that it intends to rely on its own plan. Some other provinces may decide to do the same thing. While I would be happy to see the Canada plan operating universally from coast to coast, I think all hon. members should be made aware that of all the provincial student loan plans, that which is at present operated by the province of Quebec is amongst the most generous in its terms and by all odds makes the largest number of loans.

The option of receiving equivalent compensation is, of course, available to any province. To the extent that the growing demand for such loans now exceeds or may come to exceed the resources available under provincial student loan plans, I expect that the provinces will be inclined to contemplate the operation of federal and provincial plans side by side.
The formula for equivalent compensation, while it involves certain complications, is simple in essence. At the end of each year's operation we shall add up the cost of operating the plan in the other provinces and we shall then pay to any province qualified for equivalent compensation a proportion of those costs equal to the proportion that its age group 18 to 24 bears to the same age group in the provinces where the plan is in operation.
So, to amplify just a little bit and to answer the question, there would be no suggestion of guaranteed provincial bank loans. It would be up to a province that maintained its own plan to provide the funds that would be required, which might be a quite heavy drain on its credit, and all it would receive would be its proportion of the net costs to the federal government and the other provinces.

-The national defence bill.
That has been passed by the House of Commons.
The extension of family allowances to 16 and 17 year olds who continue their education.
That has received the consideration of the house.
The bill providing for student loans.
We are now dealing with it.
The federal-provincial fiscal arrangements bill.
Third and final reading of the extension of the fishing zone to 12 miles.

The significant part of this is that parliament is away ahead of the government's expectations, because the next paragraph says:
When these items are completed, hopefully by July 22 or 23, the house will return to the flag debate-
This is the first admission on the part of a member of the government that the progress made in the house is even much faster than their optimistic hopes could have expected or anticipated. Indeed, I am grateful that the Postmaster General saw fit, in a non-political report to his constituents, to pay tribute to the efficient manner in which those prior matters in legislation are being passed by parliament.
However, there is one other matter that is of interest, because after all this question has been delayed for months. Student loans have been expected ever since the speech from the throne gave promise of their being presented to parliament, and we in the opposition have continually pressed for this legislation to be brought before parliament. Apparently it belonged to the category of legislation that was promised; the program enunciated before there was consultation with the provinces, and then when consultation took place and threats of legal action were made against the federal government if it proceeded without regarding provincial jurisdiction, changes and alterations were made.
This legislation could have been introduced a long time ago. Indeed, it is now quite late, for everywhere across our country we find students in the position referred to by the minister, of being as it were in a state of suspended animation awaiting legislation while at the same time realizing that without the legislation they might very well be unable to carry on their education. The minister went back to the earlier days of his youth and spoke of the difficulties-

Many in this house-I do not know whether he is in that category-have had the experience of having to endeavour in various fields of work to earn sufficient to carry them back to university for the next term. I had that experience for several years. I remember one year in particular when I worked in the summer as a hired man, lived on salt pork and ended up with a growth on the back of my neck that used up my entire savings of the summer. The Secretary of

State for External Affairs belongs, I understand, to a group that found it necessary to do many things to provide for an education. As the minister has said, those days have changed and today there is in all parts of the free world legislation to provide assistance to students.
I mentioned a moment ago that this legislation enjoyed a position of priority. I would not want to interpolate anything of a political nature, with the Secretary of State for External Affairs sitting opposite me, but I was impressed a day or so ago by a statement made by the premier of Saskatchewan. There is another piece of legislation that should be before the house but has been forgotten, and that is the redistribution measure. It came; an amendment was suggested by the N.D.P., and it passed away. It was a shadow that came before parliament, darkened the house for a moment and then disappeared.
Now we begin to see, in view of a statement made the other day, the reason for that. I am beginning to wonder, sir, whether this priority legislation, followed as it is to be by the renewal of the flag debate, is not based on a determination of the government to have an early election, to which I referred the other day but did not have any supporting evidence. Now I have that of the premier of Saskatchewan, who last Thursday said:
Premier Ross Thatcher said today he believed there would be no redistribution of seats in the House of Commons before the next federal election.
Mr. Thatcher said he had discussed redistribution, under which Saskatchewan could lose four of her 17 federal seats, with Prime Minister Pearson.
"He didn't flatly say there would be no redistribution before the next election, but he expressed doubt that there would be at the rate parliament is moving".
That is one of the most interesting revelations. Out of the mouths of babes comes wisdom. This legislation is part of that priority group that apparently is far more important than any question of redistribution. I would not want to exacerbate the sensibilities of the Acting Prime Minister by bringing in anything of a political nature, Your Honour, but I feel that Premier Thatcher's frank revelation of conversations with the Prime Minister indicates that that must be the purpose and the aim. That is the reason this legislation is brought in at this time, to be followed by the flag resolution; and then, in the event that there is not that submissiveness on the part of parliament to the Prime Minister's diagram, there is going to be an election before there is redistribution.
Loans to Students
The particular subject for discussion today is one of these priority questions. I listened with interest to the minister as he said, as does the bill, that $40 million a year will be made available. I am all for this legislation, but I ask this question. What is the effect of this measure going to be on the universities and other institutions of higher learning, with regard to the numbers of students? What is going to be done on the part of the government of Canada to provide, following consultation with the provinces, the additional plant, laboratory, classroom facilities and so on to handle even a small part of the additional numbers that will enter universities, when facilities are now strained to capacity in every province? What plans are there in this regard?
When we were in office we faced this problem. The province of Quebec took strong objection to the acceptance of university grants. Indeed, the amount had piled up to some $25 million by 1960. The premier of Quebec at that time was the late Paul Sauve. An arrangement was made between the government of which I had the honour to be the head and the government of Quebec whereby this matter was solved for the first time. It had remained unsolved, indeed untouched, for a period of years. During the period we were in office we increased the amount of grants, on a per capita basis, from $1 to $1.50, and in December, 1962 to $2 per capita.
The result of our interest in university education and assistance thereto was that compared with the year 1956-57, when under the then Liberal government Canadian universities received $16 million in per capita grants, by 1962-63 they received $26.3 million and in 1963-64 the amount which would have been expended was some $26.8 million. In other words we were doing something to achieve that objective which the Minister of Finance has described, giving to young men and young women the opportunity to secure education not only in quantity but also in quality.
This is a problem which must be faced. For the first time, during the days of our administration there was made available long term low interest loans to universities for the construction of student residences, which was a tremendous advance on behalf of university education in this country. We made available loans to Canadian universities to construct living accommodation for resident students, and those loans amounted

Loans to Students
in total to more than $41 million. We made possible the doubling of student residence capacity, with new residential accommodation for 10,000. We encouraged university students. For the first time we provided for the deduction of tuition fees for income tax purposes. We also provided special assistance to parents who were supporting their children at university by allowing exemptions even after the students had reached the age of 21. In addition we implemented legislation increasing the monthly education allowance for the children of war dead from $25 to $60 a month. All these things were done to reach the objective so necessary today of increasing opportunities for university education.
I am not going to put a large number of statistics on the record. I am going to suggest instead that hon. members who have not done so read the report entitled "University costs and sources of support" published in 1962 by the Canadian universities foundation. Also a further report by the same foundation and the same author, Dr. Edward Sheffield, concerning the projected student enrolment in Canada in 1976; and finally, to consult figures available from the higher education section of the dominion bureau of statistics.
Without going into detail I should like to summarize one or two projections for the future. There are today some 141,000 university students. That number will greatly increase. Indeed, by 1976 it will be more than three times what it is today. One of the reasons is not only the desire for education but, as the minister indicated, the increasing numbers in our population between the ages of 18 and 24 years. There has been a tremendous increase in this regard. The minister mentioned the birth rate. In 1951 there were only one and a half million in that age group. Today there are close to 1,900,000, and this figure will greatly increase.
Then there is the increase in the percentage of young men and women as well as older people who go to universities. In our day there was only a very small percentage of people who went beyond grade 12, but in recent years the increase in this number has been tremendous. If one goes back to 1951-52 one finds that 4.2 per cent of the population between 18 and 24 years of age were enrolled in university. By this year this figure has approximately doubled. It will continue to increase and will double again to about 16 per cent by 1976. That is

why this is one of those problems-education within the jurisdiction of the province- which we must solve.
However, university education is becoming such a vast and tremendous problem that it requires national endeavour, and that national endeavour has to assist and correlate itself with provincial action by agreement. The number of graduates of universities gives some idea in this connection. The veterans' peak was in 1951-52; the number of graduates that year was about 15,000. In 1962-63 it was 28,913, and in 1963-64 it was 32,250. By 1976 the number will be 95,400.
Not only have the numbers and the percentages increased, but as well the operating cost per student in Canadian universities has mounted tremendously. In my day one's fees amounted to $35 or $40 per year. Today they are 10 to 12 times-I am not speaking about specialized professions-what they were then. The actual operating cost of the university student in Canada in 1956-57 was $1,200. Today it is close to $1,920. By 1965-66 it will be $2,200.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are challenging figures. The operating costs of universities in 1956-57 amounted to $85 million a year. In 1962-63 it was $225 million, and the projection for next year is $325 million. These statistics indicate the need for action. What is being done is beneficial, but it is just a start. It is just a stopgap, if we in Canada are to keep pace with the ever increasing need for university graduates, in particular those in science and engineering.
How are we to finance this? Where is the money to be found? Is free university tuition practical or practicable? Shall we continue to have university students pay increasing amounts in tuition fees to meet the rising cost of university education? I do not think so. Should universities control student enrolment by making entrance standards progressively tougher? Well, I know there are some very brilliant students in this house, men who were brilliant in their university days. But I also know that some of the ablest lawyers in this country found it impossible to pass their examinations and would not have any hope of admission on the basis of present day requirements. I know, too, that some of the most successful Canadians were anything but brilliant in the days when they attended university. For some

reason, over the passing years they outdistanced those whose brilliance was apparent in their university days. I am glad to see the Postmaster General here, because he and I are in agreement on this.

Yes. The Acting Prime Minister, again free from all political considerations, has suggested Winston Churchill as an example and there are many more. 1 sometimes wonder, though, whether the fact that he was not a success as a student was due not to any lack of intellectual capacity but to the fact that he did not really like the place he was attending. It was too slow for him. He had other views. One has only to read his reports from the Malakand campaign in the 1890's, only a few years after he was unable to pass his scholastic examinations, to be confirmed in this view. He wrote reports of that campaign which in my opinion are equal, if not superior, to anything he ever wrote in later life.
But this is just an occasion when I have been diverted from my subject by a very pertinent observation. If I were to be personal about the matter, I would look over at the Acting Prime Minister and say that he is one of those outstanding examples of high scholarship who showed such promise during his student days.
This student loan plan is an attractive one. It must be recalled, however, that six months after graduation or after the expiry of five years there will be a $500 payment required plus $300 interest. I just mention this, though I am sure the minister has concluded that on the basis of the present day earnings of recent graduates this will really not be difficult to meet. But it deserves consideration. This plan is an emergency measure. It is to be supported generally, I think, by members of the house, but it does not meet the overwhelming problem of advanced education in Canada, a problem which will have to be faced if this nation is to be able to meet in the years ahead the destiny which lies before it.
I will not enter into any further particulars at this time. Various members of the opposition will deal in detail with certain aspects of the subject. I conclude by summarizing what I have said. This question of university education is in my opinion one of the greatest problems our nation faces. We, while in office, make great advances. As I have indicated, this is a further step. I think it would 20220-346

be the course of wisdom when we come back this fall for the second part of the session- if we do-for a committee of the house to be set up to consider this whole question of advanced education and postgraduate education, so that in a community of co-operation in a field which is above all political considerations the members of this house, and there are many who are interested in this subject, will be able to give a consensus of their views. This having been done, the government would be in a better position to present the question to the provinces in its national context.
This university problem and the necessity of assuring the widest and most soundly based university training to all who are qualified is not solved by makeshifts, however beneficial. This is a field in which we have fallen behind. We are 15 years, I think it is, behind the United States. My hon. friend from Digby-Annapolis-Kings has made a profound study of our position vis-a-vis that of the United States, and I believe that in the course of his remarks he will deal with this aspect of the question.

maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
There can be no doubt as to the need for legislation to provide financial assistance to young people who are desirous of acquiring a university education or higher learning. There was a time when advanced education was thought of as being reserved to a comparatively small proportion of the population, particularly for those who were interested in entering the professions or the higher echelons of business.
That is no longer true. We have now moved into a technological era in which, in order to make a good living and in order to make a useful contribution to society, a very large percentage of our population needs advanced education. This has been shown by the steady increase in the number of students enrolled in universities in Canada. The number has gone up from 62,000 students in 1952-53 to
141.000	in 1962-63. It is estimated that it will double in the next six years and may reach
480.000	by the year 1976-77.
Not only is enrolment at universities steadily increasing but the cost is going up. While the number of students at universities is going up 11 to 12 per cent per year, operating costs of universities have been going up at the rate of 16 per cent per year. Prom the standpoint of the student, what is even more alarming is that since 1957 student tuition fees have risen by 22 per cent. There
54S2

Loans to Students
is no way by which the average student can make up that 22 per cent increase. No student's earnings from summer employment have gone up 22 per cent. There has been a very rapid increase in student fees and the amount of money it is necessary to have in order to get an advanced education has been climbing steadily.
The fact is that in Canada today lack of finances is denying a very large group of young people the opportunity to avail themselves of advanced education. Dominion bureau of statistics figures show that in 1960-61 there were over one million young Canadians between the ages of 18 and 21. It was estimated by educational authorities that of that number over 20 per cent had the mental and intellectual capacity to acquire a university education. But the fact is that Qnly 11 per cent were able to attend centres of higher learning or about 114,000 young people. This means that about half the young people who could have acquired a university education were unable to do so and I think it would be a fair assumption that a fairly large percentage of them did not acquire a higher education because they lacked the necessary financial resources.
It is significant that the burden of finding the necessary money to attend a centre of higher learning is very naturally most prevalent among young people who come from homes that are in the middle or lower income brackets. The Financial Post of February 8 last carried a survey which looked into where most students get the funds to attend university. They came from a variety of sources, some from private scholarships, some from provincial scholarships, .some from money lent to students by relatives and so on; but the two large items ->y which students financed were summer work, which accounted for 28.6 per cent of all i evenue which students got, and funds supplied by parents, which accounted for 31.9 per cent. This means, of course, that where parents are not able to supply these funds students are unable to get an education.
The University of Toronto advisory committee on ex-service students made a survey. Their study revealed that whereas normally only 20 per cent of the university student population came from the homes of industrial workers, 32 per cent of the veterans came from such homes; and whereas 55 per cent of the normal student population came from the homes of professional, managerial and business people only 36 per cent of the veterans came from such homes. This helped

to establish at the University of Toronto at least that the number of students suited for university education from low income groups was significantly larger than the pitifully small number who can ordinarily obtain such an education.
The Canadian union of university students has done a great deal of work on this matter. They hired a group to make a survey for them and tried to ascertain the effects on students in Canada of the lack of financial resources. I have here a table showing the number of students who over the years have had to interrupt their education because of a lack of money. It is interesting that the bulk of them, of course, fall in the category of those who come from homes of fairly modest incomes. I can sum up their whole survey by quoting from a speech which was made to members of parliament in room 112N by Mr. Patrick Kenniff of the Canadian union of students on June 25 last. He summed up the situation by saying:
It is very significant that among students whose family income is less than $5,000 per annum, over 30 per cent are required to interrupt their university education to go out and earn the necessary money to continue. It is also interesting to note that this rate drops sharply as family income increases. At $6,000 the interruption rate is 15 per cent, while at $8,000 it is 3 per cent. Without increased student aid now, we are risking making financial means the chief criterion for a university education right across the country.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I certainly agree that legislation to assist needy students is long overdue in this country. I want to say, however, that the legislation now before us is, of course, a long way from the promises which were made by the Liberal party and by hon. members opposite not only before the election but even after the election. I have here a photostat copy of the Toronto Daily Star of May 1, 1963 with a great banner headline saying that Ottawa is going to make available 10,000 scholarships of $1,000 each for four years to students. This was announced by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing). These scholarships were promised by Liberal speakers in every corner of the country. No scholarships have so far appeared. The student loan legislation now before us is a poor substitute for the 10,000 scholarships that were promised.
This legislation is really not going to cost the government very much money. Someone asked the minister how much a while ago and he said he had made estimates and that he would tell us when the bill is in committee of the whole. On the assumption the minister

is going to pay 5 per cent interest on this $40 million, and assuming it is all lent out in any one year, it is estimated there will be a payment of somewhere in the neighbourhood of $2 million a year or slightly more if the minister has to pay a higher rate than 5 per cent. This is not a very heavy contribution toward removing the financial barriers or, to use the minister's phrase, to ensure that no competent student lacks financial support to go beyond high school.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, we are not really going to grapple with this problem until we make university education absolutely free to every young person in Canada who has the intelligence to acquire it. After all, education is no longer a luxury. Education is something which is absolutely essential to enable young people to make a living and, consequently, to enable them to make their contribution to modern society in this era of the scientific revolution. After all, tuition fees now account for at the most 28 per cent of the cost of operating a university. This means that society as a whole pays up to 72 per cent of the cost of the university education of those who are able to put up the other 28 per cent. If a student or his parent cannot put up that part which they must pay through tuition fees, then all the rest of the benefits of a university education which are provided by society as a whole are denied to that student.
Most of the modern countries in the world today are now providing free education to university students and to students going on in the fields of art, music and dramatics. In the United Kingdom, ever since the education act of 1948 and in the Scandinavian countries, even in a little country like Israel with all the economic problems which confront it, free higher education has been provided. In Israel special allowances are provided to enable a student to go to university, and there are special allowances for those who are married. Dr. Cyril James, a former president of McGill University, said this:
A young Canadian from a family of modest circumstances has less chance of getting a university education today than a youth in any other country with which I am familiar.
This, Mr. Speaker, is the most damning indictment that has ever been levelled at this country. We are years behind most of the modern industrial nations of the world. We have a much larger drop-out of students between grade 1 and graduation from university than most of the countries in western Europe and larger, of course, than the United States.

I say that one of the first things we have to do in Canada is to abolish university tuition fees. The government of Canada could do this by increasing its per capita grant to universities on the condition that the universities, in turn, discontinued tuition fees. This would be a comparatively small contribution financially in terms of the vast need. It would be an advantage not only to the individuals concerned, but for the technological development of Canadian society which in the years ahead must compete with other countries that have highly trained personnel.
I readily acknowledge, of course, Mr. Speaker, that neither scholarships nor student loans will meet the real problem of university education. The real problem of university education, over and above the things I have been mentioning, is the lack of educational facilities, equipment and trained staff. There is little value in enabling a young man to go to university if there is no classroom for him to sit in, if there are no professors to teach him and no laboratories in which to do his experiments. The crying need in Canada today is for capital to expand the university equipment and facilities. The universities have been struggling to cope with the demands. Their capital expenditures have risen faster than enrolments, because scientific courses require expensive laboratory equipment. For instance, in 1956-57, university capital costs were only $21 million. By 196162, they had gone up to $136 million. It is estimated that for the three-year period 1963-64 through 1965-66, some $800 million will be required.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it is a sad commentary on our society that we have no difficulty getting capital for supermarkets, filling stations and more hamburger stands, but we have not as Canadians been able to find the necessary capital to expand university facilities in order to train the young people who will supply the technical personnel that will decide whether or not Canada can compete in the scientific era of tomorrow.
We in this party have been arguing throughout the years that the federal government must provide social capital which is necessary to enable the universities to keep pace with the growing demands for space, equipment and trained personnel. The capital requirements are such that they are far beyond the financial capacities of the provinces. As a matter of fact, there is no reason why the provinces should be saddled with this capital cost of university expansion because the universities in the respective prov-

Loans to Students
inces train students from all over Canada as well as from outside of Canada. All the students trained in the province of Quebec do not come from Quebec. All the students trained in the province of Nova Scotia do not come from Nova Scotia. Therefore it would be demonstrably unfair to burden the people of a particular province with the capital cost of supplying university plant and equipment.
We say that one of the responsibilities of the federal government is to supply the social capital which is necessary. We have been starving the universities. If we continue to do so, we will of necessity have to limit the number of students who can attend university. If we limit the number of students in the manner we are doing now by raising these tuitions fees, the students who will be shut out of the universities will be the students who come from homes that are in the lower and middle income brackets. If there is anything that ought to be determined on the basis of individual ability and not on the basis of financial ability it is higher education. There are hundreds of thousands of young people in this country who can make a contribution to our society and can live full, useful and meaningful lives if the university facilities are available and if we make it financially possible for them to attend.
With reference to the bill before the house, in my opinion it is very largely window dressing because the ability to secure a loan under this legislation will not depend on the Minister of Finance. It will not depend on the provincial authority which grants the eligibility certificate. It will depend upon the whims of the local bank manager. It is all very well for the minister to say, as he said in his speech, that if a student is not satisfied by one bank he can approach another. Yes, he can keep on approaching banks. He can spend a week or two going from bank to bank, but what is the experience of the banks?
I do not say this in criticism, but what is happening is that every branch bank is allocated a certain amount of money per month and per quarter, which is available for making loans. It is not an unlimited amount and a bank manager is under the necessity of making the best showing he can. As the Porter commission points out, he can make commercial loans and, by charging the regular 6 per cent interest, not on the money due but on the total amount of the loans, he

can make anywhere from 9J to 11} per cent interest. I myself have seen loans that made as high as 12 and 14 per cent.
If a bank manager has to choose between lending money to a student at 5f per cent- as a matter of fact during the period that the Minister of Finance is going to pay the interest it will probably be less than 5f per cent-and making a loan to one of his commercial customers and getting a return of 9 to 11 per cent, it is not very difficult to see who is going to get the loan, because there are not unlimited funds. The bank manager has only a stipulated amount of money available for lending purposes and he is anxious to make the best possible showing he can.
If anyone doubts that that is what is going to happen I suggest he take a look at the Small Businesses Loans Act and what has transpired under its operation. That is an act which was passed by the previous government in 1960. Most of us approved of it and thought it would be helpful to small businessmen. But last fall the Minister of Finance admitted in the house that although that legislation makes available up to $300 millions in loans, in the years of its operation only $90 million has been lent out-less than one third of the money made available for loans to small businessmen.
During the Christmas recess I decided to make some inquiries as to why more use had not been made of this act. I talked to businessmen and chambers of commerce and they told me many people had made application but had not been able to get loans. I then talked to bank managers and they said to me very frankly, "If you were only allowed $200,000 to be lent out in the third quarter of the year, would you lend it out under this legislation at 5 per cent when you could lend it out otherwise and make a higher rate of interest and a better showing for your branch?" The answer is obvious.

As a matter of fact the minister is doing his best to put a good face on a pretty shabby piece of legislation. This legislation is like so much that the Liberal party brings into the house. Their whole principle seems

to be, "How little can we get away with? What can we do that will look as though we are doing a great deal when actually we are doing very little?" This is like the 12 mile fishing limit. It is like so much of the Liberal legislation that pays lip service, to enable the minister to come into the house and say we are now going to reach the stage when no young person will be denied university education merely because he has not got the money.
He ought to say there will be no young person denied university education provided he can get a bank manager who will lend him the money. He did not say that. A moment ago the minister said he could not set up lending institutions all over the country. I said he did not need to do that, and of course he does not. He has a very simple remedy at his disposal and that would have been to have co-operated with the provinces in setting up a student loan fund in each province, administered by the province. Then the federal government could turn the money over to that student loan fund committee, which committee would then be in a position to allocate the money to students in the form of loans on the basis of the need of the students and on the basis of the students being able to show they have been conscientious and will make good use of the money being lent to them.
In that way there would be student loan committees whose primary interest would be in seeing that young people get an education, rather than having the loans screened by people whose primary interest will be safeguarding their money and making sure they get the best possible return for their employer, the banks for whom they are working. I do not think it is too late yet for the government to change its mind.
I have had some experience with this question of student loans. We found that the only way we could really make sure that students got the money they needed was to do as follows. I am talking in this case of a province. The province went out and borrowed the money, put the money into a fund, and set up a committee of representatives of the teaching profession, the universities, the student body and the department of education. They made the loans available out of this fund. The only test was, did a student need it, and was the student likely to make good use of it? Those are the only tests there ought to be. But when a student has to run the gamut of the gimlet eyed bank manager, the

Loans to Students
student who is going to get the loan is ofttimes going to be the student whose father has good security, or the student whose father has an account with the bank and the bank manager wants to keep on the good side of the family. But what happens to the boy whose father has no bank account, who may not even have a father, and who has to go to the bank manager with no security, with no prospects, just hoping that the bank manager will see fit to make him a loan? The minister says that if he does not get it from one bank, he can always go to another. He will certainly be doing that; he will know all the banks in the community before he is finished.
There are one or two minor things about the act that I just want to mention before I sit down, Mr. Speaker. I am surprised that the minister has not put in the act the interest rates, but I understand from his statement that he hopes, of course, they may drop from time to time so he is going to set the rate by regulation. I am a little at a loss to understand why there should be two interest rates, an interest rate which the borrower will pay when he becomes liable, which is six months after he graduates-that rate is 5J per cent- and a lower rate which the minister expects to pay during the period that the minister is responsible for the payment of interest. After all, the federal guarantee is behind the loan, and it seems to me that a rate of 5| per cent is very high under those circumstances.
I am wondering why no provision is made here for graduate students, because certainly $1,000 a year will not begin to meet the requirements of a graduate student; and these are increasingly necessary particularly in the fields of science, engineering and medicine. At the present time the student union estimate that an undergraduate, if he is staying at home, needs around $1,100 a year, and if he is staying away from home he needs some $1,550; but graduate students, particularly if they have to go to the United States to do Ph.D. work, need anywhere from $2,500 to $3,000. These are the kind of people we will have to train if we are going to have, in turn, professors to train the other students who are going to be coming to our universities in increasing numbers.
I am wondering why there is no provision in this legislation for loans to be made by credit unions with the same guarantee that is provided here for the banks. Hundreds of credit unions all across Canada have been

lending money to students for years with the guarantee of the parents or members of the credit union, and I imagine these credit unions will continue to make those loans to needy students. Why should they not have the same guarantee in this legislation that the banks are going to enjoy? I hope that when the legislation gets into committee of the whole, the minister will be prepared to accept an amendment or introduce an amendment himself to include credit unions, because I am sure he is aware that there are vast areas of Canada now in which there are no chartered bank branches. I see my hon. friend for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp), who I am sure will agree with me that there are great stretches in the rural parts of the prairies where there are no chartered banks; where the only banking in the small rural communities is being done by credit unions. My hon. friends from the province of Quebec know that the young people there have been trained from the time they start in public school to put their money in the caisse populate.

maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: Exactly.

maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: They are used to dealing with the credit union movement. I see no reason why, if the government of Canada is going to guarantee loans to students, it should not guarantee them to the credit unions and to the caisse populate as well as to the chartered banks of Canada.

maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: There is one small matter I want to mention to the minister merely because I hope he will give some thought to it and will give us an explanation when we get into committee of the whole. I am not a lawyer, but it strikes me as very strange that in clause 2, paragraphs (b) and (k)-I know I cannot discuss the clauses of the bill -there is provision for certain things to be done by the lieutenant governor in council. Lieutenant governors in council may pass orders in council on the basis of a provincial statute. I do not know how they can pass orders in council on the authority of a federal statute. It seems to me that somebody either has a very good explanation which indeed is ingenious or somebody has not thought about it and we are liable to be in great difficulties.

maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: It will have to be ingenious, but will it be constitutional?

maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: It can be got around, of course, by the provinces enacting legislation and passing orders in council under their own legislation; but they certainly cannot pass orders in council under this legislation. This is something which should be looked into.

maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: It is the new centralist look.

maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I say that this legislation will be of some value, and I hope the minister is right and that it will be of considerable value. It will allow loans to be made, when the whole $40 million is put out in any one year, to about
40,000	students. Since these students will be at university for three or four years, assuming it is four years only 10,000 new students a year can come on to the plan. If the average length of stay of the student is three years, we will be able to take on some 13,300 additional students per year. I suggest that this is totally inadequate. To be bringing 10,000 or 13,000 or even 15,000 additional students a year into university enrolment is completely inadequate in light of the fact that we have probably in excess of 100,000 students a year who are capable of making use of a university education or training at some higher centre of learning. If it is correct-and this figure seems to be general in other countries-that
20	per cent of the age group between 18 and
21	should be university material, then we should be increasing our university enrolment by something over 100,000.
This legislation, Mr. Speaker, will not do it. This legislation is similar to giving one solitary peanut to a hungry elephant. It will help. But let the government not feel that it has dealt with the whole problem of advanced education. Let it not throw this legislation as a sop to the problem of how to remove the financial barrier to providing education to the young people of Canada. We just have not done that. This is a useful step, but the government still has to tackle the much more fundamental proposition of increasing operating grants to universities so that they can remove tuition fees. The government also has to start making capital grants to universities so that they can expand their facilities, if we are ever going really to tackle the problem of bringing Canada into line with other modern nations so that every young Canadian will be able to get a university education irrespective of the financial ability of the parents of that young person.

maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure indeed, as one who belongs to the educational profession, to
Loans to Students
speak on this bill which is before us. Certainly the government deserves commendation for bringing it in. Certainly also the principle is sound, as far as it goes. But I do not think it can be counted as anything more than the first step toward meeting the tremendous educational needs which exist in Canada. I say the principle is sound because I believe it is well that we leave some of the responsibility for getting an education up to the student himself, who has the opportunity of going on to school.
I look back in my own experience and realize that I would not have been able to go beyond high school if a very kind, dear elderly lady who was a neighbour of ours had not done for me exactly what this bill is intending to do for many other Canadian students, namely provide the money to go on to school. I was not even asked to pay interest while I was going to school, because it was assumed I would repay it when I was at work, using the benefits of the education I had received. Therefore, this is a good piece of legislation and we are happy to support it, albeit that it is only the first step and that there are some basic weaknesses in it.
As the minister has already pointed out, a number of provinces in Canada have preceded the federal government in bringing in some similar type of legislation to assist students within their own boundaries. While some of this legislation may not provide as much money as will these loans, to an individual student, in other ways it is far superior in its operation than this legislation. I think it is encouraging-and I would pass this piece of information on to the minister-that in the province of Alberta, where a student loan fund has been operating now for a number of years, they have not had a" single student default in his payments under the operations of the loan fund. I am sure that this speaks well for our young people. I think it also speaks well for the principle under which this legislation is being set up, because it places some responsibility on the individual, and very often that responsibility assists the individual in doing a better job and perhaps being more purposeful and understanding while he is in school.
An amount of $40 million in a student loan fund represents, if students use the maximum amount of loan available to them, 40,000 more young people going on to school who might not have been able to do so otherwise. However this figure, while it seems staggering, is not just as much of a windfall as it seems to indicate. Because what happens in the

Loans to Students
second and third years of this further education? Supposing 40,000 students are successful this year in receiving loans amounting to $1,000 a piece. Or let us say 50,000 students receive loans, because some of them may be asking for less than $1,000 each. When they wish to continue on at school for a second year they will require the same amount of money. Yet as I read this legislation, this amount will not double next year. This will certainly place a restriction on what at first sight seems to be a very optimistic picture.

The hon. member says
15.000	students, but it is hardly that many. It seems to me that the government will have to reconsider this because I am sure that after the first year of operation of this loan fund more than 12,000 to 15,000 students will need help.

maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
