speechtext: In a single year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: It will go up at the rate of about $40 million a year, we estimate, for the first five years, and after that it will go up at a faster rate. I thought the figure the hon. member mentioned of the number of students was not quite correct. I agree with him that the number is far too few, but we are not intending to limit it to those numbers at all.

maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
According to what the
minister says, if this year 40,000 students applied for a $1,000 loan this sum will be required again next year, which means there will be no new students next year able to
[Mr. Thompson.}
get these loans because the government will have to carry through next year the obligations made to the students this year. Certainly this limits the potential of the legislation unless the government intend to escalate each year. I think this is something which the minister must clarify and reconsider, because we have a greater obligation to students who want to go to university than just those who want loans this year and who intend to go on to finish their education.
The success of this legislation will not be known until it has been proven whether or not the students will be able to get loans from the banks; in other words, whether their credit is going to be acceptable to the banks so that the students will readily get these loans. As I read the legislation, I understand that the parents will not have to share in the responsibility of paying back these loans. If bank managers are going to operate as they do in normal commercial transactions, they will have a great problem when dealing with youngsters who are 18 years old in satisfying themselves as to the credit rating of a student.
However the need for this type of assistance is urgent in Canada. It is estimated that there are approximately 600,000 Canadians, and the figure is a conservative one, in Canada's work force today under the age of 19 years. I maintain that no young Canadian in this day and age is really fit to go out into the work force equipped to earn his own living before the age of 19. If we can assist 40,000 students a year, each year, to go on to these higher fields of education it will be a strong and substantial beginning in helping our young people to reach the standards of education they need. I do not think there is any doubt that a university education or its equivalent today is just as important in terms of job buying power as was a high school education in my day or a public school education in the days of our fathers and grandfathers. Therefore as has already been brought out very clearly by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), the greatest and most urgent need in our country at this time is to make available to our young people the education they need to carry their own load and earn their own living. I commend the government on this first step. In my opinion, something has been accomplished, albeit the principles upon which it is based are not as strong as they should be.
It was my privilege in my years overseas to assist in the development of an educational

system right from the beginning in the country of Ethiopia. During the fascist occupation of that country between 1935 and 1942 no Ethiopian national was permitted to go to school, except to a political school. So we had to begin right from the beginning when we set up an educational system in 1942 and 1943. I would draw the attention of the minister concerned to the fact that even in a country such as Ethiopia which we might, from our position, consider primitive and which is certainly undeveloped by our standards, education at all levels is free, even to graduate level, as long as the student is able to obtain the necessary marks. This is the objective toward which we all must work. It is in this light that the present legislation represents only a small beginning. Other countries are far ahead of us in providing opportunities for education.
I was startled by several statements the minister made. In referring to the method by which this student loan fund would be administered he said the students themselves would have to go to their local bank managers after getting clearance or approval from some provincial authority. Subsequently he said there would be no compulsion on these bank managers to grant these loans. And then, as if to justify that statement, he said: "After all, they will be lending out their customers' money". Surely, the hon. gentleman is not so ignorant of banking practice as to believe what he said. Or did he merely think members of this house would believe him when he made that statement? Actually that is not what is done at all. That is not how banks operate. It was certainly an amazing statement to come from a man who is charged with the responsibility for looking after the finances of this country. Just to correct him I would refer to the evidence contained in the official report of the banking and commerce committee here in parliament. As reported at page 455 in 1939 a former governor of the Bank of Canada said: "The banks cannot, of course, lend the money of their depositors". Earlier at page 398 of the same record he said: "They do not lend their deposits, of course". To hear the Minister of Finance make a statement to the contrary is startling. The hon. gentleman went on to say something about the government being responsible for the national purse, and being the protector of the nation's taxpayers. I suggest that both the national purse and the taxpayers need a little more protection than
Loans to Students
they are getting today particularly when the Minister of Finance gives us such wrong information as he did this afternoon.

maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: And after he has voted for Social Credit principles, too.

maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Some of us talk a great deal about social capital. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) referred to it this afternoon and said it was necessary for the federal government to make available the social capital required to meet the educational needs of our country. That statement is correct, because certainly if social capital is classified as being the capital necessary to develop our capital resources it is not limited only to physical resources; it extends to the capital development of our human resources also, and it is this category we are considering this afternoon. Student loans fit right into this class of capital. However as long as we are to operate under the present system which insists on taking our social capital needs out of taxes instead of from our own credit sources, our ability to meet the demand for both industrial and social capital will be very restricted. I suggest to the minister that we must mobilize our financial and credit resources to provide the capital which will be needed if the tremendous cost of interest which would otherwise fall upon the taxpayer is to be avoided. I have just made a calculation without working it out in detail and I am sure that by the time the fifth year arrives, when there will be approximately $200 million out on loan-I think, in fact, there will be much more because these loans cannot be restricted to the 40,000 students who are expected to apply initially-the taxpayers of this country will have to pay a very substantial amount in interest on this capital fund. Certainly, in ten years, when the fund will have reached half a billion dollars-and I believe it will be even more when that time arrives-interest charges will run into a couple of hundred million dollars. This is not something to be regarded lightly. Nor would it be necessary to pay interest charges if we were to use our own public bank to provide this public or social capital which we are considering. Certainly, this is one of the legitimate spheres where it ought to apply.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) has indicated the tremendous need to increase the number of our young people attending institutions of higher learning. One factor likely to limit the scope of this legislation is this. I doubt whether we shall be

Loans to Students
able to provide the physical facilities necessary to accommodate the tremendous increase in the number of students if an attempt is to be made to accommodate all those students who wish to take advantage of the legislation. The very fact that it will take time to develop these facilities will afford us an opportunity to bring in much more substantial legislation designed to meet our over-all academic needs. Again we return to the question of social capital. The cost of the physical equipment and accommodation which will go into the provision of these additional facilities will be tremendous. Under our present system we draw our social capital from the commercial or tax market, which means we, the taxpayer, are going to pay double the cost of this expansion as compared with what would be necessary if we were to raise the capital through our own public bank. This involves no small considerations, Mr. Speaker, because the status quo cannot be continued indefinitely. The pressures which are building up within our society will shortly demand that something altogether different be done.
Suppose our population in 10 years or in 1975, let us say, reaches a figure of 30 million people, as I am sure it will. Suppose that the percentage of our young people proceeding to a university education remains at approximately 1J per cent, the figure now. This means that we are going to have 450,000 university students in school within 10 years or five times as many as we have now. How can we ever meet this need with this kind of legislation or with the rate of progress we are making in meeting the need for physical accommodation for these students?
The Canadian education association, meeting in convention last year, said that the greatest need in education today is financial. This is true. But it is also true that we cannot expect to continue meeting the financial need from the pockets of the taxpayers because they simply cannot continue to bear the load. In that regard it does not matter whether the federal government or the provincial governments collect the taxes because the people are the ones who have to pay in either case.
We are fortunate in Canada that we have a tremendously wealthy nation. We have the timber, the steel, the cement, the manpower and the know-how to put all these things together to build the finest educational facilities of any country in the world and make them available to every student who wants to go on to higher education and who at the same time has the initiative and ability to do so. This is the challenge that is facing us.

The question has been asked this afternoon-. Where is the money to be found? If we are to continue to take money out of the same well from which we are taking it now, that well is about to run dry. Unless we bring in basic economic reforms there will be no possibility of our finding the money to do this job and we are going to be found guilty of robbing our own children of the opportunities they must have in order to take our places after we are gone.
Therefore I say that we must lay plans now to mobilize all our resources for the development of our nation as this nation must and deserves to be developed. The minister has said that the government, as the controller of the national purse and the protector of the national taxpayer, has these things at heart. I disagree with him very much. In a very particular way this responsibility falls on him as Minister of Finance at the present time. But I do not believe that the minister under present policies, to which he not only gives lip service but which he follows in application, is actually controlling the national purse as it should be or protecting the taxpayers' pockets either. Therefore I say that while we support this legislation in principle, while it is a first step toward meeting the needs now facing us, certainly it is only one very small step toward the ultimate goal which must be ours, that of making education available to our own children.
The suggestion of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that the government should have co-operated with the provinces in setting up within each province a student loan fund operated and supervised by the provincial government is a sound one. I think it is one deserving of the consideration of every member of the house and particularly the government and the minister concerned with this legislation. We speak a great deal about the responsibility for education belonging to the provinces. The only reason the provinces are unable to meet their educational responsibilities at this time as they would like to, and as they should, is the financial limitations that are placed upon them primarily because of the inadequate federal-provincial fiscal arrangements now in existence. In my opinion it would have been a far better policy for the government to consult first with the provinces and obtain their advice on this matter because they have had far more experience than the federal government has had in this field. I believe

they would have received this advice if the course suggested by the hon. member had been followed.
I would go even further than he did and say that these student loan funds within the provinces should have been set up with social capital from the Bank of Canada and not out of the taxpayers' pockets. A revolving fund could have been established and as students completed their education and repaid the money it would go back into the fund to be used over again. This is a very fundamental and basic principle in developing funds of this type intended to perform a similar function. The process is a continuous one. If the minister had set up this kind of fund to be administered by the provinces he would not be faced with the dilemma confronting him now in trying to figure out how he will be able to give a further 40,000 students next year the same opportunity he has made available to 40,000 students this year.
I do not intend to speak longer on the bill at the present time. We will support it because we believe it is a step in the right direction, but we would again emphasize that it certainly does not reach the goal that should be reached nor is it trying to do so by a method that would have been far more satisfactory not only to the federal government but to the provinces, and most of all to the students it is intended to assist.

maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in a debate such as this one must begin by distinguishing between the objective to be reached and the means to reach that objective.
The objective to be reached here is, of course, to see to it that those who are able to benefit from education, that is, our young people, are given access to the best educational systems, so that they may be better prepared for life.
The legislation introduced today is only a method, of course, and can only be a means to attain that end. The goal to be attained is to develop the educational field, so that our young people may have access to the various schools, colleges and universities. In order to do this, the essential factors will be, first the schools, and then the colleges and universities. Moreover, there is a need for teachers, books, material, and finally, our young people must be able to reach all these educational stages.
Loans to Students
There is no doubt that we favour the proposed objective and that we want our young people to have access, without any restriction, to the schools, colleges and universities throughout this country, and to avail themselves of the best educational system and the best teachers.
Today, one way of attaining that end is submitted to us. However, under the proposed legislation, there are no means of building more colleges or universities, developing laboratories or training a greater number of teachers.
This legislation is only supposed to be part of the general machinery of our educational system, which aims at giving our young people financial access to our educational institutions. And how do we go about it? Simply by saying: We shall lend you money up to $1,000 a year, for five years, and you will repay this loan at the end of your studies.
Education is said to mean a country's enrichment, but I wonder why, every time this country is to become wealthier in some way, either by developing natural resources or by allowing our young people to continue their studies, the only means that is found is to let them incur a debt. I find this surprising aspect in every piece of legislation submitted by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon). There is apparently no possibility of developing this country, of increasing its wealth and assets, without putting it in the red by incurring a considerable debt. A surprising fact, indeed. I cannot understand why this country could not be developed without getting further in the red.
I think we should launch an inquiry on the subject, in order to increase this country's prosperity, either by developing its natural resources or by using its human capital, without going further into debt.
And how are we treating our young people? At the end of five years, they will be graduated as doctors, dentists, lawyers or engineers, and they will have incurred a debt of $5,000, even before they start practising their profession. They will be 25 or 26 years of age and, in the case of a doctor or an engineer, perhaps even 30, if they specialize, and they will be burdened with a debt of $5,000 even before they start their career. This means that right in the first year when they will begin to practise their profession, after starting their studies at the age of four or five, and finishing them at 25 or 26, they

Loans to Students
will already have debts to pay off to the banks, as the result of loans made under this legislation.
Moreover, they will have to obtain further loans in order to buy the required equipment for their offices and, when getting on in years, they will owe fairly large sums.
In fact, in the case of a student in dentistry, he will probably have to borrow $7,000, $8,000 and even $10,000 in order to buy his chairs and all the required office equipment and, in some cases, his debts will be paid off only at his death when the insurance company will extinguish his debts with the premiums he will have paid all his life.
In my opinion, if the Minister of Finance is really eager to help young Canadians so that they might help in the development of this country, he should think of a system other than the debt system.
I note that the federal government has acquired the habit in recent years, of encouraging all classes of Canadians to get into debt. In fact, under the farm loans scheme, farmers are getting into debt. The same policy is followed in regard to rural development; again, the farmer is being involved in debt. Legislation concerning loans for industry and trade has already been passed; now we will have loans for students. The federal government has become a lending agency, which gets everybody into debt, from the cradle to the grave. And before long, there will be loans to enable Canadian citizens to borrow to pay the cost of their own funeral, because frequently families have not enough money for this purpose.
It is exactly the policy that this government seems to follow and, in order to make us forget what is behind all that, namely the continuous running into debt of the individuals, they gild the pill. In fact, the Minister of Finance did not mention any repayment. He merely said: Education must be developed. Then, in utter confusion he takes the objective for the method. As far as the objective is concerned, everybody is in favour. But with respect to the financial method, for instance, we do not agree.
Students should have access to institutions of higher learning, to colleges, universities and technological institutes. Very well. But why push them into debt? Why force those young people to start in life with a debt of thousands of dollars on their shoulders, even before earning one cent? That is what we cannot approve in the legislation before us.

And how will those loans be granted? The chartered banks will create the money to enable our young people to continue in school. But those chartered banks enjoy an exceptional privilege. In fact, when a young man goes to the bank, the manager says: "Very well, my friend, we will lend you the money you need. The federal government will pay the interest and guarantee the loan. We will lend you $1,000." Then, all the bank manager has to do is to take his pen and a piece of paper and make an entry in the amount of $1,000 in the young student's ledger. He will have created $1,000 with no more trouble than that. Then, bankers will be getting rich at the expense of students as they are now getting rich at the expense of farmers, industrialists and businessmen for whom the federal government guarantees certain loans.
That is exactly what happens. And the almighty bank, not only will keep on doing like in the past, but will also develop education in our country.
It is really a shame to see that so much power is given to that organization which is getting richer on the pursuance of public works or the development of natural resources in this country and even today, that organization is called upon to push our young people into debt even before they start in life. Indeed, those young students will start school owing a debt to the most powerful banking institutions.
And when a young professional, a doctor, a lawyer or a dentist wishes to open an office, he will have to borrow again in order to purchase the necessary equipment, and maybe to pay the rent for the first few months. The credit of the young student will be practically exhausted by then. The banks will hesitate to allow him another credit margin to open an office, especially when we know that, in certain professions like medicine, science, dentistry or business all the necessary furniture and equipment cost a lot. Then, the young professional will have the greatest difficulty to start practising and the government will have to introduce other legislation to guarantee loans to young men who have completed their studies in order to help them open an office and practise their profession. In this manner, they will be indebted all their life.
Mr. Speaker, there is another point on which I would like to insist. The measure under consideration comes after many other measures by which the federal government

interferes more and more in an exclusively provincial field as specified by the constitution, that is education.
There have been grants to universities, grants to technical schools and, not long ago, the act providing for an allowance of $10 to students was passed. Today, we are considering a measure providing for loans to students. We already have special scholarships. In fact, for a number of years, practically every session we have had before us new federal legislation increasing the intrusion of the Canadian government in the educational field.
In general, education gives rise to a number of problems which can only be settled by united action, not by piecemeal and inadequate expedients. At present, the federal government takes certain steps in the field of education and, a little later on, a province takes other steps, with the result that there is no uniformity within the educational system of the provinces. Why is this? Because too many governments have a finger in the pie.
Instead, why does the central government not transfer to the provinces part of its taxation powers with respect to individuals and corporations so that the provincial authorities may carry out on their own a responsibility which is given to them by the constitution, the development of education within their territory.
In the province of Quebec, we already have a loan scheme, a scholarship scheme. And knowing the present Quebec premier, we can imagine that this new federal intrusion in provincial affairs will enable Mr. Lesage, by accepting those new loans to students, to keep the money which used to provide loans and scholarships to students. Indeed, that is what he did when the federal government increased old age pensions and raised students' allowances by $10; he kept for himself what he used to give. It will be the same thing with those new loans.
Then, the provinces will be inclined to withdraw their scholarships and say: use the federal loans to students scheme.
There are replacement payments, but they are always controlled by the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot accept the principle of this bill. We agree with the objective of the program, but not with the method advocated, at the present time, for it amounts to another interference, on the part of the
Loans to Students
federal government, in a field over which the provinces have the exclusive jurisdiction, that of education.
After this, people are surprised to find there is dissatisfaction. Why? Because the federal government wants to interfere in fields not under its jurisdiction.
It would be much simpler, for the government, to return their sources of income to the various provinces which want them back so that these provinces could themselves develop the field of education.
But today, the opposite is taking place. It is the federal government which takes the larger part of the cake, that is, of the taxes, and which, in so doing, tries to enter fields which do not come under its responsibility. The federal government, on the contrary, should hand back to the provinces a larger part of income, in order that they may themselves meet their obligations.
In the province of Quebec, people wish to develop this field of education, but they lack revenues. Already, private property is taxed and overtaxed by school boards; the provincial government has again increased the sales tax, from 2 to 4 per cent in some cases, in order to meet the expenses for education. Despite all that, the federal government keeps the major part of the taxes and interferes in the field of education.
It would be better-and we are going to submit an amendment to that effect-if the federal government turned over to the provinces 2, 3 or 4 per cent of personal income tax and, with those amounts, the said provinces would look after student loans. The advantage would then be as follows: The provincial government, being the only one to look after education, could standardize its general programs in order to improve the educational system within the province; the provincial government could make all the decisions without having to deal with the federal government. But, at the present time, both governments are interested in the same field.
Mr. Speaker, there are several clauses in that bill which make us question its legality. Thus under section 15, even those under age can borrow as if they were of age at the time the loan is granted.
There is a civil code in the province of Quebec which comes exclusively under provincial jurisdiction. This clause is clearly inconsistent with the civil law of the province, because, once again, under the constitution,

Loans to Students
civil law comes under provincial jurisdiction. Has there been an amendment to the constitution allowing the insertion of such a clause which departs from the civil law of the province of Quebec?
There are many such clauses which are not consistent with the constitution.
For instance, under section 12, a provincial government may receive compensation payments if it does not want to take part in the over-all plan but, under that section, the ten payments will be paid to the province only six months after the fiscal year. This means that a province will be penalized for an 18-month period, that is the whole year plus another six months. In the meantime, the province will have to pay, meet costs, interest charges, and so on, during 18 months. Therefore, it will be at a disadvantage compared to the other provinces, if it wishes to get the compensation payments.
Mr. Speaker, this legislation contains things which are not necessarily acceptable. For instance, the federal government would like to have the right to determine what institutions the students wanting to secure a loan should approach. In section 13, the government would like to establish a set of rules which would be glaringly inconsistent with our Canadian constitution. It wants to reach agreements directly with the institutions the borrowers will approach. This is found in section 13.
Mr. Speaker, this legislation is contrary to our Canadian constitution, on several points.
It is often said that students need those loans to continue their studies. Well, Mr. Speaker, I would like today to congratulate the students of the province of Quebec, that is the students' federation of Quebec, including the general students' association of the University of Montreal, the general students' association of Laval University and the general students' association of Sherbrooke University. They all stated categorically that they are opposed to the federal program of loans to students. Why? Because those students' associations, which are primarily concerned wanted to put the general interest before their own personal interest. They said: The federal government must not get into the field of education, even by passing such an act.
I have here an article, which was published in the July 9 issue of Montreal-Matin, on page 10:
No loans for students: French Canadian students once again required from the federal government the return to the provincial government of the taxation powers which will enable the latter to fulfil the priority needs of the province of Quebec.

The Quebec general university students associations once more stated that they objected to any step that would promote the passage of the student loans bill, saying that such a measure, although commendable, runs counter to the aspirations of the students who are in favour of a greater provincial autonomy.
Although they need this assistance, the people primarily concerned in this are opposed to the federal government intruding further into the field of education by way of this bill.
If those most directly concerned object so much, the federal government should realize that it must find other means to reach its objective.
We readily accept the method suggested by the Quebec students and which is that the Minister of Finance should say: For the provinces which do not want this legislation, we will give them back a certain percentage of the income tax. It would be exactly the same thing as in the case of the $10 a month allowances to students of 16 and 17 years of age.
I do not see why the minister cannot provide for such an alternative in this legislation. He would thus respect the provinces' autonomy while avoiding more disputes. Why always try to make matters worse?
It seems to me that the situation is already tense enough and that nothing should be done that could make it worse. The Minister of Finance should realize that this is not the time to provoke further people who do not want any intrusion from the federal government in the field of education.
We do not want Ottawa meddling with education in the province of Quebec. We believe we are qualified to organize our own educational system; we know that we are at least as qualified as the federal government. So, why always try to provoke and arouse the anger and the opposition of the whole population of a province? That is what we cannot accept.
After that, they will complain, they will say that there are fanatics. The fanatics are not the ones you think, but those who are always trying to intrude into other people's affairs.
The constitution states clearly that education is exclusively of provincial jurisdiction. To pass such a bill is certainly to intrude into a field that is no concern of the federal government.
It would be so easy, since it is going to cost money to the banks, to draw these amounts from income sources or taxation

rights and give them back to the provincial governments so that the latter could consolidate the development of their educational system. The provinces who would rather take advantage of the federal plan would be free to do so. We do not intend to force anything upon the other provinces. If they want to keep on letting the federal government interfere with the education field, we will not object to it, but so far as the province of Quebec is concerned, we object because that province will not have it and besides, the majority of the students in that province also objected to such an interference.
I also make it a point to protest against this new intrusion into the field of loans to students by the federal government. It has been suggested by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) that these loans should be made through the banks. I think the suggestion should be taken into consideration; loans could also be made available through credit unions or caisses populates. Better still, since this is for the betterment of Canada, we should, and this is the suggestion we would like to make, allow every province to borrow from the Bank of Canada, without interest, so that every province may set up a students' loan fund.
But, what would be even better than loans would be to see to it that every province could draw from the Bank of Canada enough money so that it would have the necessary funds to improve the Canadian educational system: that is train teachers, build schools, colleges and universities, provide students with the means to live while they are studying. In short, the Bank of Canada should put at the disposal of the provinces the money they need for developing education.
The Bank of Canada must help to increase the wealth of our country, not only in the field of natural resources but also with regard to human capital. It should finance our needs through the provinces. The Bank of Canada is needed to develop our education system.
Those are our suggestions with regard to that bill. We are against it, first, because we see no point in getting students into debt before they can go out and earn a living. We feel they will have enough debts in their lifetime without being burdened with more while still in school. We much prefer a scholarship scheme, not a federal one, but one handled through the provincial governments. For that, the provinces must have the sources of income that will enable them to
Loans to Students
maintain a scholarship scheme which will help students to further their education without getting into debt.
In due course, we shall propose amendments to the act to allow those provinces wishing to do so to select another slice of income sources, either from personal or corporate income tax, so they can use those additional funds to grant scholarships to students.
That is what I wanted to say, Mr. Speaker. We will propose amendments in due course, but we are against the bill as it stands now. [Text]

speakeroldname: Mr. John N. Turner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to congratulate the minister on his presentation this afternoon and on the moderate, balanced tone with which he presented this refreshing piece of legislation to the house.

maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: That is quite a change.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
I rise, too, out of a personal interest. The riding I have the honour to represent is the home of two of Canada's leading universities. I speak of McGill University and Sir George Williams University. My riding is, as well, the site of an outstanding ladies' college, Marianopolis College. At these three institutions over 30,000 students pursue daily their studies toward a recognized degree. I would say on my part and on their behalf that the principle behind this legislation, the principle that talent and admission to university should not be denied by reason of financial straits, is one appropriate to justify the approbation of every member of this house. I would say, too, that it epitomizes what this government and this party is trying to achieve in the way of equality of opportunity; that any young man or woman who has the intellectual qualifications sufficient to gain admission and retain admission in a university should be able to pursue a university course of education; because as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) pointed out, a university education today is no longer the luxury it once was but is a necessity, a necessity not only for those who seek to make a contribution to this country later in life but a necessity for the country in that the skills of our young men and women are surely the prime asset this country has.
This legislation, therefore, is an investment, an investment in the intellectual capital of Canada in that it will achieve a bettering

Loans to Students
of the skills of our young people and thereby increase the spiritual and intellectual assets of the country. I would hope this would encourage more young men and women at an earlier stage in their lives to point toward a university education so they may help us build up a Canadian bank of brains. I would say to the minister that I would hope any inducements he has made toward encouraging research in Canada, toward encouraging those who have achieved university status and the status of a degree in Canada to remain in this country, will be continued; because the purpose of this legislation, which is to bring into the academic institutions of Canada more of our brains and develop more of our brains will not be fulfilled, not only if we do not have the physical plant to service this potential but if we do not retain in Canada the young men and women who are able to take advantage of this legislation.
I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) making his constitutional argument. Coming as I do from the province of Quebec and representing, in so far as their university studies are concerned, about 30,000 students who pursue their studies in that province, I would like to deal briefly with the constitutional position a little later on. Before I begin that analysis I would say that I think the constitutional argument is now an academic question in that I am satisfied that the rights of the provinces have been adequately fulfilled and that Premier Lesage, who once threatened to take the proposed legislation to the courts, has now no reason to challenge the legislation. In fact I am going to suggest that in his own bursary and loan plan as developed under the department of education he has a wider, more generous plan than that offered under the present federal legislation. I would think that in view of the fact that the province of Quebec now devotes over one third of its annual budget to education, it will be the intention of his government and the intention of Mr. Gerin-Lajoie, the new minister of education, to maintain the standards of the bursary and loan plan and to increase the services, the eligibility and the amounts payable under that plan. Taking the academic argument for what I now think it is-that is to say, academic in the sense that it will not entail any practical problems for the legislation-I would think the Canadian government has a responsibility under the general welfare provisions of the British North America Act to the youth of the country to increase the skills of our youth. Just

as the federal government has a responsibility in the area of manpower retraining so as to meet the threat of automation, so also have we a duty to see that our youth is skilled sufficiently to survive and prosper in an automated and complicated age.
It should be noted that the subsidy, if subsidy there is under this legislation, attaches not to any educational institution but to the individual. We are living in a mobile society where students tend to get their education often in provinces other than those from which they come. We are now dealing with a payment largely along the lines of the welfare payments which attach to individuals, and this surely would constitute a powerful argument in favour of a federal jurisdiction.
Indeed, we have the general banking power under the British North America Act. Clause 3 of this bill makes it clear that this enabling section authorizes a bank to assume responsibility for loans to students, such loans being guaranteed by the federal government. Clause 15 is a recovery provision authorizing the bank to recover the repayment of a loan. In passing, might I say I could not agree more with the hon. member for Red Deer in saying that we anticipate very little failure to honour loans under this legislation. The experience of those provinces and institutions which in the past have maintained provincial bursary or loan schemes is such that it is found the rate of repayment is almost 100 per cent. As to the legal ability of a bank to pursue its rights under this particular legislation, any discussion while proper is probably academic in view of the record of students in this country who have in the past honoured the repayment of their loans.
On the other hand, I recognize that the provinces have a strong constitutional argument on their side. But I repeat that my conclusion is that the argument has been satisfied and reconciled. The argument advanced at the federal-provincial conference by the province of Quebec when discussing this subject was that this item fell under the head of education within the meaning of section 93 of the British North America Act by virtue of the remission of the interest payments during the tenure of the loan. While a student is at any university, and until six months after his graduation or withdrawal from university, such remission of interest in effect constitutes a subsidy for the purpose of his continuing his education. This is made clear in clause 4 of the bill.

The second argument advanced by the province of Quebec was that that province, as indeed other provinces like Saskatchewan, Alberta and others, was already in the field. I believe that in the year 1963 over $18 million was advanced by the province of Quebec under its bursary and loan plan to students; and roughly 50 per cent of those moneys were advanced in the form of bursaries, the other 50 per cent being in the form of loans. According to the official brochure put out by the government of Quebec, 40 per cent of the bursaries are repayable and in effect might be treated as loans. Taking this mathematically, if 40 per cent of the bursaries are repayable and the bursaries constitute half of the money advanced, roughly 65 to 70 per cent of all moneys advanced by the province of Quebec to students is in effect in the form of loans.

I understand the usual ticklish impatience of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), but I said earlier that the plan of the province of Quebec is a remarkably fair and generous plan, and its terms of eligibility are wider in many respects than those of the present plan. Since 70 per cent of the moneys disbursed by Quebec is in the form of loans, it seems to me there should be no difficulty when it comes to working out the mechanics of making loans or distributing loans to students who travel from one province to another, in dovetailing these two plans.
I have mentioned two arguments in favour of provincial jurisdiction, namely that this matter falls under the head of education and that the province of Quebec was already in the field. A third argument underlying those two is the feeling that if an item falls under provincial jurisdiction, and if education is a crucial factor in maintaining a provincial autonomy, then there should be the constitutional power and the necessary resources to allow the provinces to fulfil that jurisdiction. To that opinion I subscribe.
Let me say, after posing the constitutional positions as I see them, Mr. Speaker, that this bill satisfies the constitution of this country. First of all, clause 10 allows any province
Loans to Students
to designate the appropriate authority for the issuance of a certificate of eligibility to a student. In other words, the province, as the minister has said, will act as a partner of the federal government. In the case of any province which decides to set up its own provincial student loan program, as Quebec already has, clause 12 of the bill makes it quite clear that that provincial right is maintained in its full sanctity. I rely too on the expression of intent of the minister when he said that the federal government has no intention of superseding any plan now in existence, and I interpret that to mean any provincial plan now in existence and certainly any plan privately endowed.
I have said that Quebec already has its own plan, and I understand that it is the intention of that province to maintain and continue its plan. On reading its terms of eligibility I feel confident that the students in the province will receive equal or better treatment than those in the rest of the country.
This massive attack designed to improve education standards in the province from which I come is succeeding to such an extent already that there are enrolled in universities in Quebec 10,000 more students than in the province of Ontario, and with this impetus I have no hesitation in saying that students who attend universities in my riding, and indeed in the province, will be well looked after.
Speaking to the bill itself, may I say I think it is a commendable and good beginning. I do not agree with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), if I may say so with respect, when he calls it a makeshift. I think it is an admirable inauguration of legislation which will I hope be improved over the years. I would have wished to see the term "student" defined more broadly. Under the terms of this bill a student must be a full time student at a post-secondary educational institution. This disqualifies part time students, and particularly night students. I hope that in future years eligibility will be widened. I hope that the precedent which was set in the recent amendment to the Income Tax Act whereby tuition fees paid by part time students were made deductible, just as those paid by full time students are, will be followed in this field. I hope we shall see the day soon when part time students and particularly students attending courses at night will be able to take advantage of this legislation. I might say that provision to this end is made in the

Loans to Students
law and regulations of the province of Quebec. This is an important area of education at university level. In every large city of this country a growing proportion of those attending university are not doing so full time in the day time but are doing so in their leisure time at their own cost at night. Of the 30,000 students who attend McGill and Sir George Williams Universities, more than 15,000, that is more than half, attend those institutions at night. I would imagine that similar figures apply to universities in the other major cities of this country. I realize the difficulty attached to making a beginning, but I would urge the government, in passing, to widen the eligibility under this measure.
I think there may be problems concerned with the mobility of our students and I hope the mechanics of arranging for students from one province who attend universities in another can be satisfactorily worked out. I do not wish to continue at any greater length. I congratulate the minister most heartily on his tremendous inauguration, a tremendous advance in the legislation of this country. I commend this bill to every member of the house hoping that we all recognize that it constitutes perhaps the first positive stimulus provided toward increasing the skills of our young people and encouraging them to advance to higher education.
The result of this legislation will be that young men and women having the necessary talent and qualifications regardless of their financial resources can now be assured of a university education. I interpret this as bringing us a step closer to a society in which equality of opportunity will be realized and this is of particular importance in a society in which success depends in such a great measure upon access to education. I hope too that this will be a stimulus, through true constitutional means, to any province which wishes to administer and manage its own plan. I think it satisfies the needs of a mobile society and the need for certain national educational standards. By this I do not mean national administration. I mean an equality of standards from province to province. I think it must also be a fulfilment of what we have called in this house cooperative federalism and I hope that members who enjoy debate will recognize that it preserves provincial autonomy and jurisdiction over education.
In closing may I say that I am sure the students of this country are immensely en-

couraged by what has been said today and by what is envisaged in this legislation.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Gordon for the second reading of Bill No. C-110, to facilitate the making of loans to students.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had an interesting debate this afternoon on the matter of loans to students and for a few moments I should like to discuss the matter further. I am not going to deal with any details of the bill itself. During the debate this afternoon there were references by a number of speakers to

various matters of detail which I think are important but which in my opinion can be much better dealt with in committee than in the house.
There are problems of constitutionality. I am not speaking of the educational prerogatives of the provinces. I think there are one or two sections of the bill which might be questioned vis-a-vis constitutionality. There are one or two sections the legal implications of which I think are rather dubious. However, these matters can all be dealt with much more adequately at the committee stage and I do not propose to deal with them now, important though they may be and quite properly referred to by some hon. members who have preceded me.
We have been dealing primarily this afternoon with the problem of the individual student. Other than the speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), who referred to the general problem, other speakers dealt primarily with the problem of the individual student. It is a real problem and one could spend a great deal of time in discussing it. One could spend a great deal of time discussing just what comprises a university and the place of the student in it. I think it was Aristotle who, we are told, taught under a tree, and that was a university. When I survey the problems with which our universities are confronted it seems to me that our problem is not only to find the tree under which we are going to teach but to find the teachers who are going to operate under the tree.
I think it was Stephen Leacock who once said that the way to establish a college is first to find a teacher, then to get a smoking room and then to find the students thereafter. That may be a rough paraphrase of what Leacock said but generally speaking I think that was an apt description in his humorous way of the founding of a university.
Our problem today is not to find students to enter the universities. Our problem is to find the universities which can accommodate the students. That is the primary problem and it is in that regard that I should like to speak for a very few moments tonight. The suggestion has been made today that in the past possibly universities were the prerogative of the sons of the rich, that this measure is going to solve that problem, and that there will now be an open sesame whereby the sons of those not so rich or those who are in relatively poor circumstances will be accommodated in the universities. Personally I do not accept that statement at all. I am sure there are numerous members in this chamber who were
Loans to Students
not sons of the rich but who entered university and graduated therefrom, although perhaps with some difficulty and some hardship. That has been the tradition of our educational system in the past.
I can think of someone I know who was lucky enough to get a job as housemaster at a school for the blind at $25 a month and free room. If one wants the privilege of eating with the blind day in and day out, when they are really blind, even a stomach which is attuned to overseas service may find it a little bit difficult when you first enter that environment. But that is part of the background of which I am sure many hon. members have had experience.
The bill before us has an impact upon the individual and to that extent all of us welcome it. We know that there is a need for increasing opportunities for education. We welcome the bill. As I said, there are details in it which we can criticize and which we will criticize when we go into committee. But certainly the party to which I belong and I am sure all members of the house welcome the bill as such and are glad to see this additional step toward the educational development of this nation.
Having said that, we cannot overlook the problems which are flowing in upon the universities of this country today. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner) referred this afternoon to his association with universities in his own riding and their great traditions. In a very small way I have been associated with a university as a member of the board of governors for 20 or more years, and I know something of the problems of a small university as well.
I think we can all appreciate the problems with which we are confronted. The truth of the matter is that there has been a phenomenal growth in the student bodies of our universities during the past few years, a growth which has taxed the universities to the utmost. Prior to the outbreak of the war the combined registration of the universities of Canada was approximately 35,000. That number had gradually built up during the years as Canada progressed. Immediately following the war, with the influx of veterans with the preferences they obtained from the government, the student bodies of the universities increased to a total of approximately 83,000. This was a really phenomenal increase and every university was taxed to the

Loans to Students
utmost. Basements were used. Every possible type of accommodation which could be found was made use of. But it was done.
Following the influx of the veterans registration dropped off fairly substantially, not to the pre-war level but down to about 67,000. This year registration at our universities is approximately 158,000 students, male and female. When you consider that growth in that short time, you can envisage the problems with which the universities are confronted today.
Projections perhaps can be inaccurate. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) will recall that when he was chairman of a royal commission quite a few years ago he projected the student registration for this year. His estimate was considerably less than that which has ensued. As a matter of fact, every estimate, every projection of student registrations for these years have been substantially lower than the actual registration. If the projection of the conference of Canadian universities for 1970 is accurate we will have a student registration of 312,000 as compared with 158,000 today. This, Mr. Speaker, is only six years from now. If history proves, as experience has in the past, that this projection of 312,000 students is an underestimate rather than an overestimate-and this is without any stimulus such as is proposed in the bill we have before us-and is based on the assumed growth in population of this country, then the problem is acute indeed. If we assume the regular gifts and contributions which universities have received, the scholarships and bursaries, the usual accommodation which students are receiving today, and if we are facing a student body of 312,000 in 1970 under existing circumstances, and if the figures of the Minister of Finance are correct as to the effect of this $40 million-I am certainly assuming they are-then, you can see the terrific strain that is going to be placed upon our educational facilities within the next few years.
As I said, we welcome the bill in so far as individuals are concerned. However I suggest this is not any solution to the problem of education in Canada. We have to go much farther because actually we are facing an increase in registration of approximately 12 per cent per year and at the moment we have not the facilities to accommodate the students which we have today. The growth is going to be very much greater. I am sure the Minister of Finance would not be surprised to hear that I saw a brief, a copy of which I am sure was distributed to all members, from
[Mr. Nowlan.i
the university conference suggesting that in three years from 1963-64, the capital demands on our universities for the normal expansion to which I referred will be over $800 million. It is assumed that the provinces will probably advance roughly $300 million; there will be gifts from corporations and individuals of roughly $100 million; there will be loans for construction purposes of another $100 million, which would make $500 million in all. This still leaves a shortage of $300 million to be raised to take care of the mere physical requirements of the universities.
Speaking of the loans, I should emphasize what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Dief-enbaker) said this afternoon. These loans are, of course, under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for housing accommodations and provision was made for them by the government of which I had the honour to be a member. I referred a moment ago to the relatively small university with which I have been associated for many years. This university is now contemplating borrowing $900,000 just to increase its residential accommodation. I hope, and I expect as a member of the board, we will be able to get most of that money from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to provide the additional residential accommodation which is required. Tenders are to be called tomorrow or the day after tomorrow for a million dollar library. A great deal of that money has to be raised by loans.
This means that $1,900,000 will be required for a relatively small university which a few years ago was accommodating 400 or 500 students and now is accommodating 1,500. The demands are still growing. Applying that little yardstick with which I have intimate personal knowledge, and the same problems to a greater extent apply to all the universities of this country, you can see something of the demands on the physical capacities of universities. A Liberal government of a former year under Mr. St. Laurent, as I recall it, gave $50 million to the Canada Council on the condition that they would lend or give this to universities, provided there were matching grants of an equivalent amount. In that day, when demands were not nearly as great, this was a real bonanza, a tremendous help to the universities of this country.
As I said a moment ago, if this estimate is correct and $800 million has to be acquired within the next three years, and if there are $500 million available as suggested, this

still leaves $300 million to be acquired. I suggest that possibly the Minister of Finance might consider following the same pattern followed by a preceding Liberal government, and make matching grants available so that this $300 million can be raised by dollar for dollar contributions from the federal treasury and from the grantors or donors to individual universities. I am speaking quite hastily, so this is a very rough outline of the physical demands, a minor pen sketch of the physical demands which are going to be required under existing circumstances, forgetting altogether the impact of this bill upon universities in the next few years.
I have been speaking of the physical demands. However as Aristotle exemplified, you get the tree and you get the teacher. Where are you going to get the professors and the teachers to meet the requirements of this burgeoning student body? The problem is not an easy one to solve. Perhaps in the field of arts, with increases in salaries, you can bring forward a certain number of teachers and professors to meet the demands. However in the field of science, with the competition from the United States, the competition from national defence laboratories where technicians, particularly physicists, are in the greatest demand, you have a great problem which is going to be very difficult to solve. Heretofore we have been fortunate; we have been bringing professors and teachers from Europe, emigres who wished to escape and who were well trained in the sciences. They were coming here, but that source of supply is pretty well finished. We now have to look for professors, teachers and instructors, to people trained in our own universities.
The province of Ontario I think is making a contribution towards this end. They are providing scholarships and loans to those who are prepared to enter the teaching profession, and as a condition of accepting these loans these people must enter the teaching profession. This would cover professors and instructors for universities. I think there, too, we can consider not only loans to students, desirable as they may be, but if we are going to solve this educational problem or make even an approach to it, we will have to do something to induce more and more graduate students to enter the teaching profession, because there are so many fields today which have their financial appeal that it is very difficult to meet the demands being made.
I read the other day that we are only graduating enough teachers-professors-that if they all stayed in this country they could only
Loans to Students
accommodate the present student body, without any possibility of meeting an increase in it in the future. If the figures I gave the house a moment ago are correct we shall have to double the teaching body during the next few years, and we are not going to do that by simply increasing the student body, desirable as that may be. Somebody, whether it is the government, private institutions, corporations or the provinces-and I suspect it is going to be a combination of all of them-will have to provide inducements for a terrific increase in our teaching body if we are going to attempt to deal with the demands for teachers.
Very hastily I have referred to the capital and to the problems of the teachers. What about the current problem, about the current demands and the deficits which every university is running up today? Despite the generous contributions, despite assistance from governments these demands and deficits are increasing. The government of Canada started to give assistance with grants based on 50 cents per head of the population of Canada, on a provincial basis. That ratio was raised under the aegis of the former government and under the aegis of the government preceding that, until today it is $2 per head for every person in Canada. But I suggest, Mr. Speaker, it is based on an entirely wrong principle. It is based on the population of the provinces, and the provincial population is not increasing anything like the increase in the student body. The student body is increasing at over 12 per cent per year, and we know the factors which have entered into this, such as the birth explosion, the post-war marriages and so on. It is because of these we have such a terrific increase in the student body, but still our grants remain based on population per province.
I think it was a wrong basis to start with, and perhaps I am a little selfish in saying that; but every province could give the same example. In Nova Scotia we have no provincial university, even though we have more universities per capita than any other province in Canada. There was a time when some consideration could have been given to amalgamating them but that time is long since past and now we have several, relatively small but very efficient and very good universities. Yet up until a year or so ago we had no provincial grant whatever from the province, and we were based on grants of 50 cents per head of the population, $1 per head, $1.50 per head and $2 per head, which is the present figure, and the universities have had to seek all the gifts they could obtain.

Loans to Students
Because of the obvious high quality of those universities down there they have been getting students from Ontario, Quebec and all the other provinces of Canada. The law school to which I owe a little allegiance was recognized at one time, and possibly still is, as the best law school in Canada, attracting people from all over Canada to come down there as students. We have a large number of students from the West Indies. We have them from China, from Hong Kong and from various places throughout the world; but of course we get no credit for that whatever because we receive this payment on the basis of the population of the province, even though a large part of our student body may be coming from outside the province. If there is any unjustifiable system by which grants are made, this is certainly one which should be considered and revised in the immediate future. Because of that special problem of the maritime universities I draw the minister's attention to this fact, and I know he may well say to me, "Of course, you may have heard of that while you yourself were sitting over here." That is true, but there were factors which entered into the situation and the minister knows them well.
All universities in Canada are facing great demands; we recognize that. Yet the conference of university presidents unanimously recommended to the government of Canada, last year and again this year, that there should be a special increase in grants to the universities of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick because of the peculiar situation in which they find themselves. They recommend that pending a general revision of the basis to which I referred a moment ago, there should be an increase in the grants to Nova Scotia universities to $500,000 a year and an increase in the grants to New Brunswick universities to $300,000 a year.
When you get university presidents with all the justifiable demands made upon them, meeting in conference and coming to the government with requests to meet their own situations, and yet they unanimously join in a request for special consideration to the universities of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, then I suggest there must be some real merit in the proposition they put forward or else they would never have joined in that appeal.
I am not going to take any more time of the house except to suggest that these problems I have mentioned, the fiscal, the current and the teaching problems, all require special attention and there are none of the answers
[Mr. Nowlan.l
to those problems in this legislation. Desirable as it is, worthy as it is, if it is successful- and I am sure it will be-it will simply aggravate the problems because it will create a larger student body and therefore greater demands on the fiscal, personnel and current problems of the universities in Canada as a whole.
My hon. friend from Burnaby-Coquitlam suggested this afternoon that the time had come when all university tuition should be free, that this was only a pourboire and that we should give free college tuition to everyone. That is a question which might be debated, a question which may have merit, but I do not think we have reached that stage yet. We have too many pressing problems at the moment, problems which I have outlined very briefly and very hastily.
Over-all, this country has a problem in education. It is not only a government problem, it is one that concerns the provinces, individuals, corporations and the federal government. It is a problem too big to be dealt with without the active co-operation of and a greater degree of assistance from the federal government than we have had heretofore. Much as we may welcome this bill today we are simply skating over the surface of the problems of education facing this nation, and I think the time has come when we have to evaluate the demands being made upon us.
Only the other day we had the royal commission on health reporting to us, and incidentally when you read that royal commission report you can see just one of the problems. You cannot proceed with the health scheme it recommends until you build larger and better medical schools, until you find more medical professors and teachers, and a problem of 10 years duration is going to ensue before that facet of the educational problem is met, assuming we can start meeting it tomorrow morning. That is only one of the problems with which we have to deal, and that is one of the demands being made on us for a health scheme which will be very valuable, very helpful and of great assistance to everyone.
We have a pension scheme just coming over the horizon, as we know, which presumably is going to provide security for everyone in their old age. Then we have this educational problem, which is a very pressing one. I quite agree with what everyone said here this afternoon, that the greatest asset this nation could have is a well trained, well

educated youth. Without that we cannot get ahead but, as I say, we have to evaluate the demands of these competing services.
Yesterday the Minister of Finance, dealing with another problem, said there should be conferences to cover taxation problems. The right hon. Leader of the Opposition advocated a general conference to deal with all the problems with which the nation is confronted. Whether we adopt the idea of one conference or a number of conferences the time has come when there must be a serious study given to the problems of education. It must be evaluated as against other demands made upon us. This bill we have before us tonight, which we will all support, is one step along the road; but the fact that we take that step creates other problems which must be dealt with in the near future.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, very briefly I wish to recommend that the bill before us this evening should receive the unanimous and speedy approval of this parliament. To keep our nation strong we must encourage an ever larger percentage of our youth to attend institutions of higher learning. If we do not, we shall very soon lag far behind the nations of the western world. A university education is a prerequisite to an increasing number of positions in business and industry as well as in the professions and the public service.
The Canadian union of students maintain that only one half of the young people who are capable of higher education ever enrol in a Canadian university. They assert that such waste of human talent is indefensible. Few will disagree with this judgment. Student loans will not solve this problem, but they will help. This bill merits support only on the basis of half a loaf being better than no bread at all. In fact, compared to an adequate program of scholarships or the elimination of student fees entirely, it is a very poor half loaf indeed. During the immediate post-war period thousands of our best students would not have been able to go to university except for the grants they received through the Department of Veterans Affairs; and today many of the young people who need help are the sons and daughters of veterans who themselves were assisted by the federal government at the end of the war. I wish grants were available to them on the same basis as applied to their parents, but this is not so. There are very practical reasons why university attendance is beyond
Loans to Students
the reach of many good students in every Canadian community. Let me list some of them:
1.	University fees are being increased year by year; living costs remain high. The minimum amount required for a girl or boy living away from home is approximately $1,500.
2.	Good paying summer work is scarce in many parts of the country because of chronic unemployment; part time employment during the winter is difficult to find.
3.	Hundreds of excellent students fail to qualify for the few scholarships that are available; they need help.
4.	An increasing number of students are married and accordingly have family responsibilities.
5.	Students are frequently required to travel to another province to secure specialized training or to pursue postgraduate work.
All these factors and others should be kept in mind in deciding whether or not students are in need of financial assistance. Another point that I should like to emphasize is that arrangements for negotiating loans should be directed by university administrators who have experience in dealing with students. Direct contact between students and banks should be kept to a minimum. Loans should not be hedged about with requirements and conditions that may be embarrassing and discouraging to many deserving young people I was glad to learn that no guarantor was needed, and not even the consent of parents.
Although loans are not a substitute for scholarships, let us make them as easily available as possible. Separate arrangements with those provinces which may prefer to expand their present programs is most commendable. In this way, delay can be avoided and benefits made available at once. This parliament should not withhold from any young person in this land the opportunity for the fullest possible education. With this thought in mind, let us not delay the passage of this bill in the hope that many students will be able to take full advantage of it this year.
