speechtext:
We hear that our legislation is too late; it is too late already. The right hon. gentleman's words were that this legislation concerning the student loan program is too late also. But we should listen to the words of Mr. James G. Mitchell, president of the students council of the University of Waterloo and Mr. James D. Kraemer, chairman of the board of external relations of that university. They said this in a letter they sent to me:
The Ontario legislature did not adequately meet the needs of her expanding universities and as a result there has been a widespread increase in tuition fees (a situation common throughout Canada). The increase in fees (which in our case amounts to more than $75) coupled with the growing scarcity of summer employment once again threatens to make "university" a "privilege of the wealthy".
Earlier in their letter they say:
Our earnest hope is that the members of parliament will effectively expedite this priority legislation-
That is referring to the student loan program now before parliament:
-which awaits the house, in order that a system of federal loans for students will be in effect for September, 1964.
Education today is one of the major public services in Canada and is absorbing an increasing share of the total revenues of all governments. Expenditure on education takes a very high proportion of provincial and municipal revenues, and this affects directly and vitally the public finances of the provinces and municipalities. The federal government's finances are also subject to strain as potential additions to federal revenues are

reduced by increasing provincial and municipal levies and as the federal government is requested to assist increasingly in financing education.
It is generally felt that all have a right to obtain the level of education which they are able and willing to achieve. Education today is a door opening up opportunities for all individuals, but it is also a pathway, I suggest, to a nation's economic growth and development. It is becoming realized generally that education is an important factor inducing national economic growth as well as enhancing individual potentials. Universal education can be provided only by public authorities, and all levels of government, I suggest, need to co-operate in framing national education objectives and devising appropriate methods of financing the level of education which it is deemed we can afford in this country today.
In the modern society of today it has become essential to pay attention to the development of our human resources and skills. Failure to utilize these to capacity is a loss, not only to the individuals concerned but also to the economy of this country. One of the greatest challenges faced by modern society is to develop the full potential of its human resources, and virtually every country in the world shares this challenge.
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner) earlier today commented upon the constitutionality of this program. As we all know, section 92 of the British North America Act sets forth those matters which are the sole responsibility of the provincial governments, and included among them is education. In the field of education the problem of intergovernmental division of responsibilities has grown rapidly since the turn of the century, when the total expenditure on education was about $10 million per year. Between 1951 and 1961 the expenditure on formal education increased from $516 million to nearly $1,800 million.
Expenditures on formal education are still increasing rapidly and in 1963 it was expected that this would exceed $2,300 million. By 1981 it is expected likely to exceed 7 per cent of the gross national product. This I submit includes not only the cost of students' education, but operational costs and capital costs to the universities themselves.
Everyone is aware of the rapidly increasing enrolment at universities and colleges. The number of persons of university age is rising

at a high rate and is increasing proportionately every year. At this university age level, a greater proportion are going to universities and colleges today than ever before. It is becoming increasingly necessary for young people to take higher education in order to qualify for the top and middle ranks of positions in our society.
It is further to be noted that the number of students engaging in graduate studies is increasing at an even greater rate than the undergraduate enrolment levels. University enrolment increased from 86,800 in 1957 to over 141,400 in 1962. The sharpest increases are still to come as the population bulge resulting from the great increase in births in the immediate post-war years is beginning to reach university age level.
Many young people too are having difficulty obtaining employment because of lack of training. Vocational training has been provided by public school boards for many years. The federal and provincial governments have recently been providing vocational training, and very recently the federal government began a crash program in co-operation with the provinces to provide complex training facilities throughout the country.
Before the post-war period the main federal contributions to formal education in this country were in the field of Indian and Eskimo education, and some small grants to the provinces for vocational training. During the postwar period the federal government began to contribute to higher education-I mean by that university and college education-under a scheme to assist war veterans, and capital grants to universities were introduced in the 1950's. Many of us recall, certainly I do, that when we first attended university there were a large number of veterans who had returned from the war and were taking advantage of this grant to aid their education and to receive training at school.
At the university level students are charged an annual fee varying from $200 to $700, depending on the institution they are attending and the faculty they are entering. The cost of textbooks and students' supplies must be added to tuition fees, so that the total education cost imposed very considerable financial burden on many students and their families. Scholarships and fellowships and bursaries help, I submit, offset these costs for many students, but these are not sufficient, and insufficient students are able to take advantage of these scholarships, fellowships and bursaries.

A survey was made of university and college students enrolled in selected faculties for the academic year 1961-62, which survey was to analyse expenditures and sources of income. This survey showed that for a single male undergraduate living at home the total expenditure during the college year ranged from $1,060 to $1,652 per year. Those not living at home spent between $1,406 and $2,321. Expenditures for single female undergraduates were slightly lower than those for males. Married undergraduate students spent on the average-and it is interesting to note this figure-from $2,758 to $2,929. Male unmarried students at graduate level, therefore, had an average expenditure of $1,598 for those living at home and $2,035 for those living away from home. This is quite a sum of money, Mr. Speaker, when you realize that most of these university undergraduates come from families of low income. Married male graduate students spent on the average $3,968 during the college year.
It is also interesting to observe that in a brief submitted by the Canadian school trustees' association to the royal commission on taxation the following passage appears at pages 30 and 31, with which I agree:
With the high degree of division of labour and mobility of the labour force which characterizes our society there is a continuous pressure to have education expenditures covered to an increasing extent by the national government. What is required in a federation like Canada is much division of labour among the three levels of government in providing and financing different kinds of education.
We suggest that the local governments be primarily responsible financially for elementary education, assisted wherever required by the provincial governments-
The federal government could assume much of the responsibility for vocational and higher education, in co-operation with the provinces.
The brief further goes on to say:
A suitable system of student loans or bursaries could be worked out in such a way that no individual with the required capacity would be unable to borrow funds for investing in his own education. The repayments would have to be stretched over a long period of time, perhaps over most of the working life of the individual as in the case of house mortgages. Such a scheme would be superior to the usual scholarship systems which are limited to the relatively few outstanding students and are largely financed from public funds. The loan scheme could be available to all students who could meet entrance and passing requirements and would provide substantial private sources of funds as repayments were made.
These conclusions were arrived at by the Canadian school trustees' association in their

Loans to Students
submission to the royal commission on taxation, and it would seem to support 100 per cent the type of student loan program which is now before the house.
This legislation, Mr. Speaker, is no giveaway measure. It makes it incumbent on the student to repay money made available to help him and her pass through university or college. It should instil, I submit, a sense of responsibility and at the same time remove the unfair yardstick of making financial means the only criterion for education. Many students have to take jobs to help finance their way through college. Many of us in this house have had to do this, myself included. There is nothing wrong in this during the long summer vacation, but summer jobs today are harder and harder to find for university students. My own experience this past summer has given me evidence of that. Many university students willing to work are finding it more and more difficult to place themselves in jobs and it is becoming more and more difficult to find jobs open. When one speaks to personnel managers who previously set aside a certain number of jobs for university students, the answer he receives is: We have just so many jobs for them; we cannot open any more because we have to make room, and logically so, for these people who are displaced from our industries by automation and technological change. Therefore it is becoming much harder for a university or college student to obtain summer employment, and therefore the student loan program will assist him in this regard. Further, Mr. Speaker, students are forced to do part time work during their semester years, and this can seriously interfere with their studies. Because of this a student may be prevented from producing his or her best results.
I believe the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) mentioned the fact that more than 30 per cent of the college students from the lower income groups must interrupt their schooling for at least one year to earn tuition money. This is a waste of valuable time and energy. The federal government, with this legislation, can now take a great step forward to alter a state of affairs which has plagued students for so many years.
It is true, as has been said by many speakers on the other side, that this is not a program which will solve all the problems of the students and of the universities. Of course it will not. But it is one step forward

toward a solution. We remember the heavy inflow of immigrants in the post-war years, the years immediately after the war. Today the families of these people are of university age; many of them are leaving secondary schools and are eligible for universities and colleges. In many cases their families are not able to put them through courses of higher learning. It is true they can borrow from the banks, and that some of these students will be able to win scholarships and bursaries. However, the great majority would not be able to continue their education, through lack of funds. This legislation will come as a special benefit to them. I know that many people in my own riding will be able to take advantage of this program and send their children to colleges and universities to get a higher level of education than they themselves were able to obtain.
This program is another forward step by the present government, implementing as it does the second of four promises to young Canadians in the field of educational opportunities. The youth allowance bill has been passed. That is one promise which was made and which was carried out. The student loan promise has been made, and we are now about to carry it out. The scholarships program is a promise which I submit will be carried out also. In addition there are the per capita grants to universities which are now being discussed.
Today machines and automated programs are performing an ever increasing number of routine, repetitive tasks, thus reducing job opportunities for untrained workers while at the same time opening up new fields for highly skilled personnel. Studies conducted by the national employment service have clearly demonstrated that there is a distinct relationship between lack of education and unemployment. I think no one with an awareness of the increasing complexity of our labour market and the distinct shift from the unskilled segment of the labour force to semi-skilled, skilled and technical workers as well as professional and managerial workers will question the value to the individual Canadian of a high level of education.
I, too, wish to support the argument put forward by my hon. friend for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner) on behalf of part time students attending universities. In my own alma mater of McMaster University there are thousands of night time students taking extension courses. These people work

during the day and the money they earn is set aside to pay for their education. I think it is proper that at some future date after this bill has been passed the government should give consideration to including among those who qualify under this measure these part time students who take these classes, often at considerable sacrifice, to advance their own education, and I suggest the welfare of this country. This principle was recognized in an amendment which was recently made to the Income Tax Act and I submit that these people, as well as full time students, well merit the advantages afforded by this type of student loan program.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the last war, education, and more particularly secondary or higher education, has developed tremendously in this country. In the province of Quebec, there has been an extraordinary effort, especially since 1959-60.
It began with the famous Barrette bills, during the 1959-60 session, and the effort was maintained under the following administrations, so that today, for the first time in Canada's history, the province of Quebec has a larger budget than Ontario with regard to education. The fact is rather extraordinary, considering that the province of Ontario has a million more people than the province of Quebec.
Today, one only has to talk with the young Quebeckers in our respective ridings to discover the craze and enthusiasm of our young
20220-347J
Loans to Students
people for education, and more particularly for technical education. Everywhere in Quebec, our engineering schools, our technical schools, our institutions of higher learning, our high schools of commerce, and various other scientific schools, are doubling and even trebling their establishments over the years.
We often hear, Mr. Speaker, that there is, at present, a terrific atmosphere, and that all governments should encourage this trend among our young people.
Doubtlessly, such an effort requires considerable sacrifice, financial sacrifice on the part, not only of the provincial governments, but of the institutions themselves and, more particularly and directly, on the part of the parents, because our fellow citizens, whoever they be, all agree that it would be a great tragedy if it should happen, that, in 1964, a talented young man in Canada were financially unable to continue his studies at a university. I am convinced that all people of good will will see to it that such an eventuality does not take place, here, in 1964.
The aim of the legislation before us tonight is to enable some students in our universities to obtain the necessary loans for continuing their studies. To my mind, this legislation will not meet with much opposition on the part of hon. members from the other provinces, except Quebec. On the contrary, I even believe that it will be rather enthusiastically welcomed. But, in the case of the province of Quebec, the situation is somewhat more difficult, because there is a rather delicate constitutional problem involved.
As a matter of fact, the premier of the province of Quebec, Mr. Lesage, made a somewhat violent statement when this question was raised. He even threatened to resort to the courts in order to have the constitutional priority of the province acknowledged in that field.
More recently, we saw with a certain amazement that the students' associations of Laval, Montreal and Sherbrooke Universities, as well as the association of the students of classical colleges and teachers' colleges send to the Minister of Finance a resolution protesting against this intrusion of the federal government in the field of education, which is essentially provincial.
These students, as well as the provincial government, expressed an opinion which is not new and which is that such loans should come from the provincial government.

Loans to Students
I must admit it is with much hesitation I rise tonight to support the bill before us.
I do so after having carefully studied the various sections of the bill, for, needless to say, before supporting it, I believe it is my duty to express serious doubts on the constitutional aspect of this document. On the other hand, I am not too surprised to see that this legislation was introduced by a Liberal administration. We have been used, in the past, to see Liberal governments always trying to interfere in the provincial fields: they never missed an opportunity to weigh down the scale in favour of the central government and to enter, with all kinds of flimsy excuses in a field which is not theirs.
No doubt, we all know that section 93 of the British North America Act, makes it crystal clear that education comes under provincial jurisdiction, and not only that education belongs to the provinces, but that they have an exclusive right in that respect.
What does an "exclusive right" mean? It is a right which is our own. An exclusive right is one that lies above an ordinary right and which even transcends a priority right or a relative right. In its own framework, an exclusive right becomes an absolute right.
But rights alone are not enough. There must be means to exercise them. This is undoubtedly where the federal government is keeping on centralizing, where it is following the line it laid down long ago, that is always try to intrude further into fields where it has no jurisdiction whatsoever. But since it holds the purse strings, it can use a little blackmail and reach its goals.
Many people will no doubt find this speech somewhat academic; they will find that these essays on the constitution are not practical enough. Personally, I see very practical applications here. That is why I have serious doubts about the legislation before us.
First of all, the federal government definitely lacks the organization to look after education. From time to time, the federal government introduces into the house enticing pieces of legislation concerning a particular field or a group of citizens; but since it has no department of education, no agency or crown corporation which might supply it with the required information so that it could decide whether or not such and such a step is necessary in a province in order to help education, one is entitled to ask why the government wants to intrude in this field. One is also entitled to wonder if this intrusion by the federal government will bring happy results for the population as a whole.
tMr. Balcer.]
In brief, the federal government intrudes in this field on the excuse that it has the means to do it, that it is somewhat easier for it to control the field, because it controls the monetary system, and so on. It collects taxes for this purpose and uses its credit for a particular measure intended to help education. This is what it is doing through this bill.
Fortunately, this bill includes an alternative payment formula. I shall give my opinion later on that subject, but I revert to my argument to the effect that the federal government does not really have the organization to look after education, to lay the foundations of the various pieces of legislation concerning education.
Consider the position of the provincial government. There you have a department of education and all the required experts. It is there that budgets and programs are prepared. It is there that the balance sheets of the various institutions are reviewed. It is there that there are meetings with the authorities of the higher education institutions. In short, the provincial government is really equipped to know what are the priorities in the field of education in the province.
That is why one may have misgivings about this bill and wonder-and here I speak as a citizen of the province of Quebec-whether this is what we really need at the present time in the province of Quebec. Is it right for the federal government to pledge its credit to the amount of $40 million in order to offer loans to students? It may be that the most necessary need, the most urgent need is the construction of laboratories, the training of university professors, the establishment of new teachers' colleges, the setting up of new libraries, a change of program, and so forth.
How can we tell? Only the provincial government can. As I said, the federal government is really not in a position to decide. That is why I think the federal government is taking a chance in going into that field. As a matter of fact, the federal government which preceded us, had gone into university grants in an absolutely disastrous way, and it is the province of Quebec which was deprived, for several years, of those amounts of money, simply because the then federal government had no replacement payment formula to enable the provinces to accept university grants.
Fortunately, this legislation, because of the opposition from Quebec, I am sure, provides for a replacement payment formula. I hope

that this formula will give the expected results. In short, I hope that this option system which certainly offers great difficulties from a constitutional point of view, will not place the province of Quebec in an inferiority position or will not completely upset the scholarship program of the provincial government and will not hinder the cause of education in that province.
The option system surely gives rise to great difficulties from a constitutional standpoint. It should not be used by the federal government as a roundabout way to keep on intruding slyly in matters where it has no jurisdiction.
However, as the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) explained yesterday, this option formula is not without merits and we should support it instead of simply penalizing a non-participating province.
Those options are conditional payments. They should merely be replaced by unconditional equalization payments. Then, we would not be trampling on the constitution but allowing the people of the various provinces to benefit from those surplus funds the federal government seems to have and the provinces could use that money to promote education.
There is no doubt, as always, that with such priority measures we are venturing into fields of activity where the needs are most pressing, in the education program of a given province, to achieve better results. For my part, I wanted to make that reservation about the constitutional aspect of the measure now before us and I must say that, because of the options provided for under section 12 concerning repayments, well, I shall support the bill while making a strong reservation from a constitutional standpoint.

Mr. Speaker, the bill now under study is certainly a very important one, since it concerns our Canadian students. This afternoon, the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) said very appropriately that the bill had a certain object in view and was advocating a certain method, and of course there is quite a difference between the methods used even if the aim to be attained is commendable.
When considering the contents of the bill, it is easy to realize that it does not at all fulfil the promises which the government made to Canadian students. In the first place, loans were to be interest free up to full repayment while the present bill provides just
Loans to Students
the opposite. A 20-year old student borrowing $1,000 per year during five years, when he will have reached 25, that is when his studies will be completed-or that part for which he will have borrowed up to $5,000-will be starting his career with a $5,000 debt. All the ministers and members will admit that it is quite shameful and discouraging for a 25-year old man to have a $5,000 debt.
Measures have been passed and suggestions have been made in the past to help our young students. Now, this legislation provides that a student who will have obtained a loan up to $5,000 will be compelled, six months after the end of his studies, to begin paying the interest on that loan, since the government will then stop paying it. On the other hand, if he takes five or ten years to repay this $5,000 loan-the minister has not even mentioned the interest rate. It is reported to be 5f per cent. Now 5f per cent over a ten-year period means that the student will have to repay $7,500 for the $5,000 be obtained.
Mr. Speaker, the essential point is this: let us suppose that the student is 25 when he completes his studies and is unable to find employment for a year or 18 months. Will the government then introduce a bill to help unemployed persons just out of university at the age of 25 and unable to repay those loans?
This afternoon, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) also stated that we shall have to resort to banks which only lend the deposits entrusted to them. I do not hesitate in the least to say that if the Minister of Finance really means what he asserted this afternoon, namely that banks only lend the depositor's money, he is not competent to hold his present office. The minister is lying not only to members of the house, but to the whole country.
The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) recalled that the former governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Graham Towers, stated before the committee on banking and commerce in 1939, that banks cannot lend their depositors' money.
I shall give an example to the Minister of Finance, because being a chartered accountant, he should know all about accounting.
An industrialist goes to a bank to borrow $100,000. The manager asks him if he has any personal collaterals, such as insurance policies, redeemable securities and often asks him to produce his marriage contract, not to take away his wife, but to ascertain if she will become the owner of his properties after

Loans to Students
his death. In any case, the manager takes all necessary precautions and finally agrees to make a loan of $100,000. Immediately, he asks him to sign notes, papers, collaterals, etc., covering the amount of $100,000. Then he creates a credit in favour of the borrower for an amount of $100,000, and this is entered into the books. Before the industrialist came to the bank, this $100,000 did not exist in the books. And to prove it, if we add up all the bank accounts that existed before the industrialist went to the bank and add them all up again after he left, the Minister of Finance would see that the bank accounts total $100,000 more than they amounted to before the industrialist went to the bank to obtain a loan.
Where is this amount of $100,000 coming from? Let the Minister of Finance inquire from the Bank of Canada. Let him inquire from the chartered banks of Canada who are authorized to create credit, who not only have the right of creating credit but the exclusive control over credit for the whole Canadian people. Then, we are told that bankers lend the money of their depositors, the money deposited in private accounts. When the loan for $100,000 was made-I see that the Minister of Fisheries finds this very funny, he does not understand anything, but he still finds it funny. People often laugh at this, but they do not know why they are laughing.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance was not speaking the truth this afternoon when he stated that bankers were lending the money of their depositors. I should like to draw his attention-

Mr. Speaker, as far as education is concerned, the only conceivable solution, which would respect provincial rights as well as individual rights and more particularly the rights of our young people, of our students, would be to make available to provinces credits, established by the Bank of Canada, without interest of any kind, not a kind of education, an indebted education, a kind of education which, in 15 or 20 years hence, will be entirely controlled and dominated by the Canadian chartered banks.

And why will the students take advantage of this loan plan? Because at present, they cannot fulfil their obligations. Therefore, advantage is taken of this and a plan to directly socialize education is proposed which would be controlled by the Canadian government and Canadian finance.
Today, automobiles are finance controlled, furniture is finance controlled; nearly everything is finance controlled, and we will now have finance controlled education for our children. What a beautiful system the present government is setting up in Canada.

they will not be able to repay their debts. Then, the federal government would no longer pay the interest; the students would have to pay it six months after completion of their studies.
That is not what the Liberal party promised the students during the 1963 election campaign. Students were promised scholarships and loans without interest. The Liberals did not tell the students they would have to repay the loans six months after having completed their studies. The Liberal government hopes to get out of it like that, but I am convinced it will not. We will not allow future generations to get into debt as the government is now advocating. Mr. Speaker, I should like, first of all, to pay tribute to Mr. J. A. Richard, a former member of parliament for St. Maurice-Lafleche, who died this morning.
Born in a poor section of the province, at St. Gregoire, and forced to leave school at an early age to earn a living, he built up, by dint of hard work, a going concern in Shawinigan and served his municipality as school trustee and alderman, and was active in charitable organizations.
At an age where most people think of retiring and living comfortably on their private income, Mr. Richard agreed, at 62 years, to run in the general election of 1949 and he remained in the public service until June 1962 as member for the constituency I am now representing.

Loans to Students
His friends from St. Maurice-Lafleche and his colleagues in the House of Commons remember him as a hard working, honest, devoted and sincere person. May he get his well deserved reward.
During the present session of the legislature, the province of Quebec gave itself a department of education. A man decided to provide his fellow citizens with the instrument they most sorely needed to ensure the fulfilment of the French language, an adequate educational system. That man was Paul Gerin-Lajoie. He succeeded in convincing the people of Quebec that, as far as economic standards are concerned, the only way to catch up with their most important neighbours, the United States and Ontario, was to train competent people who could play their respective roles in the community. And now, I feel it is my duty to say to the whole of Canada that thanks to that dynamic action in the field of education, Quebec and French Canada are preparing themselves for the mission which is entrusted to them in this country. We no longer want to be silent partners in the economic expansion of Canada; we want to be in the van. At present, Quebec is investing more in its human resources than Ontario whose population is larger by one million. "Operation education" has been launched. Quebec is on the march and we are proud of it.
For us, Quebeckers, education is the field where we are most concerned about our prerogatives and, under no circumstances will we tolerate any intrusion in that sector. The survival and emancipation of French Canada depend on education, and we will fight for our rights in this regard to the last ditch. If we want to survive, we must be intolerant in this matter.
This being said, we must recognize that the bill concerning student loans brings into confrontation the jurisdictions of two different governments. The federal government is responsible for credit control, but education falls under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces.
I hope that nobody will deny that education is exclusively a provincial matter. Anyone questioning that would get one biting answer from all hon. members of the province of Quebec, regardless of their political affiliation.
In all fairness, we must also recognize that, in the past, the federal government enacted legislation in many fields to provide credit

for citizens in all parts of Canada. I will mention just a few: small businesses loans; farm loans; Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loans; loans to municipalities; loans to fishermen; university grants and assistance to technical training.
Now, the government is well aware of the problem that comes up in this legislation, that is the possible conflict between two different jurisdictions. Having understood that difficulty, it has prepared its bill so as to remedy that problem.
In the past, when the federal government grappled with any legislative problem, it did so without any or with very little regard for the opinion of the provinces in a given field. The central government used to take a rather lofty attitude which was likely to set public opinion against it.
Now, with reference to Bill No. C-110, the government first wanted to know the views of the provinces at the last federal-provincial conference, and the Minister of Finance pointed out this afternoon that several provinces-and I say several, because too many people think only of Quebec-informed the federal government that this came within their jurisdiction and they would not tolerate any unwarranted intrusion by the federal government. However, the federal government obviously had to enact legislation on behalf of those provinces which were anxious to provide their students with the necessary funds to continue their studies but which were unable to do so because of the large size of their population, their financial position or various other reasons. Once the provinces had expressed their views on the project submitted by the federal government, the Minister of Finance prepared a bill in accordance with the two following principles which are of the utmost importance:
(a)	education comes under the provinces while credit is a matter of federal jurisdiction;
(b)	the recognition of the contracting out formula under which a province may withdraw from the scheme without sustaining any financial loss.
The first principle-provincial jurisdiction in matters pertaining to education-is clearly recognized in section 10 of the bill which
states:
-the appropriate authority for a province may issue or cause to be issued a certificate of eligibility.

In addition, paragraph (b) of section 2 gives the following definition:
"Appropriate authority" for a province means such person, body or authority as may be designated by the lieutenant governor in council of that province as the appropriate authority for that province for the purposes of this act.
Accordingly, it will always be the provinces which will designate the students eligible under this legislation. Consequently, it is quite clear that the federal government does not infringe upon the field of education since control of the scheme will rest in the hands of the body chosen by the province and the latter will always be free to entrust its department of education with the administration of the program. Furthermore, in order to cover any province which is not convinced that it is in its interest to take part in this plan, the government has included in the resolution a second principle, mentioned above, namely: the possibility for a province to contract out and to receive in return an equalization payment; this illustrates the new philosophy of co-operative federalism.
As a matter of fact, section 12 of Bill No. C-110 specifies that a province that will not participate in the program will get an amount per student equal to the cost the federal government pays in all the other provinces.
I think this is a major change in the attitude of federal legislators to such an extent as to improve understanding in this country.
That being said, what must Quebec do in view of this situation? First of all, it is important to state that the effort made by Quebec in the field of education must be continued without faltering. But you must not forget a principle brought forward by the party I represent which, at the provincial level, was saying in 1960 that not one student in Quebec should abandon his studies because of financial difficulties.
That is why I would urge the province of Quebec to give serious consideration to this bill, so that it can benefit thereby to the fullest extent possible.
However, there is a point which I find important and which I consider to be a victory for a group of members of my party who have been advocating this for months. I refer to the fact that it is entirely up to the province to decide whether or not to take part in this program. That decision is left to the province. No province is obliged to participate. I think such a change of attitude should make my fellow citizens in the province of Quebec very happy.

Only two years ago, such a provision in federal legislation would not even have been considered possible.
It is by putting up a positive and intelligent fight that Quebec will succeed, and not by resorting to demagogy and irresponsibility.
At the federal-provincial conference other provinces raised objections to the bill now before us. However, I was glad to learn this afternoon, from the Minister of Finance himself, that, now that they have been informed of the formulas advocated by the present government, some provinces would be ready to reconsider their positions.
If my province, after having considered the bill in every detail, does not consider it constitutionally objectionable as an impingement on exclusive provincial jurisdiction in matters of education, I hope that the students of my province, like other students in this country, will be able to benefit by this formula.
I think, if our governments could agree on this project, that Canadian unity would immediately benefit. If there were uniform opportunities, while maintaining the unquestionable prerogatives of the provinces, some English speaking students who do not reside in the province of Quebec would be able to go there to study and get a better knowledge of the French element in Canada. I think there would be a considerable advantage in uniformity, as there would be an advantage to French speaking students who would want to study in another province to acquire a culture which suits them.
I submit that this bill is something new. It is a historic bill, because, for the first time we have a piece of legislation containing all the provisions needed to help the provinces fully avail themselves of their autonomy, while permitting the application throughout Canada of a policy which would be of great service to the people.
I am not afraid to say that there is no political impingement in the educational field by the federal government at this time, because the final decision, according to the provisions of this bill, is not in the hands of the federal, but of the provincial governments.
I hope that the Canadian provinces will try to make use of this plan as we must not indulge in vain constitutional conflicts either on poverty or on education.
What we want is to give Canadian citizens the greatest opportunities we can so that our country will be a united country where every

Loans to Students
citizen will be in a position to achieve the objective he has in mind without being deprived of education.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few remarks on the bill now before us. First I should like to say how strongly I support this type of legislation. I am one of those who believe that the only limiting factors in an industrial society such as Canada's in furthering one's education should be the individual's own ability, capacity and application. This legislation seems to me to go a long way toward equalization of opportunity for our youth. I would expect it would receive ready support from all members of the house, particularly from the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Rheaume) who spoke so strongly last night in favour of equalizing opportunities in Canada. I would hope the official opposition would not oppose such an equalization measure, as they did the Family Allowances Act.
I am also one of those who found it necessary to skimp, to save and to borrow in order to get through university. While worry and privation may possibly contribute to self-reliance, we should not delude ourselves into
[Mr. Cantelon.l
thinking that many students can be successful in this way. It only takes a very short illness, a month without a job or some other unforeseen circumstance to place the dream of a university education completely out of reach of the student who is trying to make it entirely on his own. With rising tuition fees and living costs, I doubt that it is possible to work one's way through college nowadays, particularly if the student is taking an engineering course, an applied science course or if he is in medical school or any of the many other fields that require 35 to 40 hours of lectures and laboratory work a week, in addition to studying and preparing the reports that the student is required to submit.
I believe that the students of Canada are only asking for an opportunity, not a subsidy, and in my view this plan will go a long way toward solving a growing national problem. I want to remind hon. members, however, that this loan plan is not an end in itself but should really be regarded as only a beginning, a first step, if you will. I want to urge the provincial authorities to give top priority to the provision of more university facilities for our growing student population. This legislation will make it possible for more students in our society to attend university, and we are already faced with the problem of overcrowded facilities in most provinces. In my opinion this is a problem which is reaching crisis proportions and I would urge the federal and provincial governments to give it top priority.
We also have a critical shortage of trained university staffs and we must deal with this urgent problem which threatens to limit all our efforts in this field. We are currently spending thousands of dollars to train young people, only to lose them to the United States because of the limited opportunities for research and the lower salaries which are paid in Canada. We provide our youth with free public and secondary school education. We support them through state supported universities. We support them through scholarships, and now we are going to support them through loans so that in many cases they can find better jobs and opportunities in the United States.
In view of the technological changes facing our North American society, the revolution in which we are now involved and the need for trained and skilled minds in such a changing society, in view of the shortage of staff and of facilities, the lack of research opportunities and the difference in pay scales between Canada and United States, I urge the

government to convene a conference with the provincial authorities forthwith, or at least to place this matter very high on the agenda of the next federal-provincial conference in order to tackle what I consider to be a problem of national concern.
One aspect of this legislation is that it may help to solve another very serious and related need in our technological society. I refer to the low incidence of postgraduate students at Canadian universities. I should like to quote from an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail in early February of this year. It deals with a brief submitted by the Ontario council of university faculty associations to the provincial government outlining the seriousness of the problem. The article reads in part as follows:
Of the many points of powerful argument made in the excellent brief of the Ontario council of university faculty associations presented to the government several weeks ago, not the least is the story of the deficiency of Ontario and, indeed, of Canadian universities in graduate education. University education has two facets which are not always recognized by the public-undergraduate study and postgraduate study.
Later the article goes on to state:
It is from this latter group that professors and other university teachers are ordinarily obtained, and also the top scientists and research staff used in industry. University education is generally considered impossible without these highly qualified people-
The ratio of graduate to undergraduate students in Canadian universities is ridiculously lower than in universities of similar national importance in the United States. For instance, Harvard has about 60 per cent of its students in graduate work- The university of Chicago has about 68 per cent; Columbia about 60 per cent; Yale and Princeton, 50 per cent; University of Michigan, 35 per cent; University of California, about 30 per cent.
By comparison, (the latest figures from the dominion bureau of statistics are for 1961-62), the University of British Columbia has a ratio of about 6.8 per cent graduate students; Alberta, 6.3 per cent; Saskatchewan, 4.4 per cent; Queen's 9.1 per cent; McGill, 12.3 per cent; Western Ontario, 13 per cent; and the University of Toronto, about 9.3 per cent-
The article continues:
We cannot hope for very much from the other provincial universities in Canada-the biggest outside Ontario, the University of British Columbia, had its provincial grant heavily cut by the Social Credit government last year-and it can be seen from the above figures that the production of university professor material is on a low level in the others.
If we are to produce the staffs we are going to need for the universities in Ontario, which are expected to triple in size of enrolment in less than 10 years, we shall have to invest very heavily indeed in graduate schools of all kinds. This need is probably more urgent than any other phase of the university crisis.
Loans to Students
The approach of this crisis was made known to the Ontario government 10 years ago, but it did nothing about it when there was still time. About a year ago, Premier John Robarts set up a scheme for fellowships for advanced study by graduates of Ontario universities, and provided a modest capital sum for planning further facilities. It is necessary to enlarge these funds substantially. The difficulties of the situation ought not to paralyse action.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this brief really points out a national problem, one which merits the attention of all levels of government and certainly of all members of this house. I believe this legislation is a significant step because it can be used not only by the student who needs assistance during his undergraduate years but the student who wishes to take postgraduate work. It can be used by the student who feels he has been a burden to his parents long enough and feels he should begin to pay his own way. He will now be able to apply for a loan under this plan to continue his education.
In my opinion, there is also perhaps the further need for an incentive to encourage the student to take postgraduate training after four years or more of toil with no income. Once having gotten him through a postgraduate course, either here in Canada or in a university in the United States, there must be some means also for encouraging him to return from the United States. It was with this in mind, Mr. Speaker, that I placed a motion on the order paper on February 27, motion No. 38 which calls for the granting of a tax free period to the successful student for each year spent in accredited postgraduate study. This would provide an incentive to our trained people by way of an opportunity to recapture the costs incurred in these studies.
A further result of this scheme, Mr. Speaker, would be to keep highly trained minds at home, or alternatively to bring back to Canada students who are Canadians and who are doing postgraduate work at universities in the United States. They would return to Canada in order to benefit from this tax concession. In support of this idea, I would remind hon. members that it has been estimated that it costs approximately $50,000 to train a Ph.D., and most of this money comes from public funds. I also feel that the period during which we are likely to suffer the greatest loss of trained minds is in the period immediately following graduation, when the student has not incurred any family obligations. He has not earned any seniority or pension benefits with

Loans to Students
a company. He has not earned any promotions with a Canadian company. He is therefore very susceptible to the higher starting salaries and to the higher grants given to research in the United States. I therefore urge that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) consider this suggestion of mine. I hope that we might see it in our next budget.
I think it would play a very significant role in keeping these highly trained minds in which we have a tremendous investment of public funds here in Canada, in order that they may contribute what they can to our economic development.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the same factors apply in the academic world. Certainly, the need for university professors, the need for trained people in our universities, would also be helped by such a measure. I should like to place on the record some of the views regarding this very serious strain of our human resources which have been appearing in our newspapers in recent months. I have here an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail from which I should like to quote:
A disturbingly large number of these Canadians who move to the states have obtained costly education and training here. The House of Commons was informed this week that in the 12 month period ending last June, a total of 1,583 highly trained persons-mainly engineers, but including scientists, university teachers, physicians and surgeons-left Canada for the United States. For the previous year, the figure was 1,295; and for the year before, 1,270.
I should like to quote from the Globe and Mail for Tuesday, April 21, 1964:
The brain drain of Canadian university professors to the United States was blamed here yesterday for contributing to a shortage of specialized international study courses in Canadian universities.
Dr. J. F. Leddy, a professor at the university of Saskatchewan, told a special meeting of the national conference of Canadian universities and colleges-
There is more in this article and I could go on, but I have already quoted from the brief of the Ontario council of faculties of Canadian universities, indicating the need for a threefold increase in university staffs in the next ten years.
I was interested also in reading an article in the New York Times commenting on the furore in Britain over this same problem, which by contrast with our own on a per capita basis is really very minimal. Mr. Wilson, the leader of the Labour party devoted a major political broadcast to this exodus of political scientists. He is reported as follows:
He scored the "miserably inadequate provisions by the government of research facilities" and said

that even when a British scientist scored a breakthrough "it is left to American or other business firms to build the industry that this British discovery made possible."
Mr. Wilson said about 140 Ph.D.'s were leaving Britain every year permanently, a lot of them for the United States. He said this was nearly one in eight of Britain's yearly output of highly qualified scientists-
Government officials, smarting under the criticism, are suggesting that Prime Minister Sir Alec Douglas-Home will raise the issue with President Lyndon Johnson when they meet in Washington.
I think the New York Times comment was indicative of the seriousness with which this problem is regarded in Britain. Certainly, the problem in Britain is really insignificant compared to the per capita problem we have here in Canada. I would strongly urge that the federal government and provincial governments take note of this serious problem which I feel is limiting Canada's ability to compete in this highly industrialized and complex world.
I would ask the Minister of Finance to look seriously at the notice of motion currently on the order paper in order to determine if it could not be used as a further means of attacking a problem of national significance.
I commend the government for moving quickly on this loan legislation. I suggest a further step could be taken, perhaps in the next budget, by the adoption of my motion. I strongly urge that a conference be held with the provinces concerning university facilities. This latter problem must be given priority, even ahead of student scholarships, of which the opposition has been making much. I feel this problem of the facilities which we are able to provide for the greater student population is a much more urgent one and one which requires the full attention of all levels of government. I would ask the Minister of Finance strongly to urge the cabinet that this be placed as one of the top priority items for the next federal-provincial conference. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this whole problem of advanced education is becoming such an urgent one that our next step must be planned very carefully indeed, and in my own mind I feel that the problems of the facilities and the staff are much more urgent than anything else.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING OF LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, considering the requirements of modern science and the need for higher education which our young people must have today, the government takes this

pretext tor introducing legislation which, at first sight, may have a great appeal, which may be understandable, for the majority of hon. members, but which, in my humble opinion, is quite unacceptable to the province of Quebec. And I propose to give hon. members the legal grounds.
The end does not justify the means. When introducing this legislation, the government cannot, ostensibly due to the magnitude and complexity of the problem, make a constitutional issue out of it, when education is under exclusive provincial jurisdiction under the British North America Act.
Today, federal-provincial relations are reaching a dramatic turning point in Canada, in the fields of taxation and of responsibilities. A conference should be held to decide whether we must come back to the federal system, with the sharing of powers and responsibilities, or whether we should continue, by all possible means, to realize a Unitarian system which will assume all responsibilities, absorb the majority of the taxation fields and act as a distributing clearing house, whereas the provinces will become vassals or branches of this Unitarian system, the policies of which will be dictated by the central government under the guise of national importance, national scale or national standardization.
It is interesting to hear discussions about co-operative federalism. Since our hon. friends came to power, they have been trying to find a camouflage for their centralizing feelings which always characterized Liberal administrations under the King and St. Laurent governments.
Later on, in my remarks, I intend to deal with that problem, referring especially to the problem of the setting up of assistance or grants to universities and legislation which was brought forward in 1951, while Hon. Mr. Cass, said: If we push assistance to universities too far, there will be a subsequent necessity for the federal government to go into the field of elementary and secondary education.
There is no doubt whatsoever that cooperative federalism is used as a smoke screen by our Liberal friends. It is a new formula, as during the last war, when the new phrase had been coined-people spoke no more of conscription, but of mobilization. Today, we speak no more of centralization, but of co-operative federalism.
Canadian federalism is a system of association between independent governments, that is the governments which practise it are coordinated but not subordinated to each other.
Business of the House
However, under such a system of association, these governments co-operate in the common duties, such as mentioned in article 95 of the constitution, with respect to immigration and agriculture. These governments must respect each other's exclusive rights.
Under such an association system, the same governments know they cannot do indirectly what the constitution forbids them to do directly. As a matter of fact, the privy council in London gave a decision on that point, as well as the supreme court.
The federal government is now trying indirectly to intrude in a matter directly under provincial jurisdiction, that is, education. Through the legislation now before us it is trying to do indirectly what it is prevented directly by the constitution.
Indeed, that principle of Canadian federalism has been recognized and approved many times by judgments of the privy council in London. I am sure the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau), the Liberal leader for Quebec, who has held high administrative posts, had the opportunity to read those judgments, and especially the Great West Saddlery case (1921), the Edwards case (1930), the Aeronautics case (1932) and also the unemployment insurance case (1937).
May I call it half past ten?

THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-STEPS TO MEET REPORTED INCREASE IN COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of today's sitting, I put a question-I regret that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) is leaving-but I am sure that his parliamentary secretary (Mr. Pennell) will give me an answer.
I directed a very significant question to the Minister of Finance as follows:
What measures does the minister intend to take in order to stop the rise in the cost of living, since Montreal has already recorded the highest rise?
The city of Montreal is among the ten metropolitan areas covered by the dominion bureau of statistics the one which has recorded the highest increase in the cost of living from May to June 1964.
In fact, the increase in Montreal was 0.9, the index rising from 134.3 to 135.2 while in Toronto it was only 0.7; however, it must be pointed out that in the latter, the index is the highest one in Canada, that is 137.1 compared with 136.4 last May.
Mr. Speaker, the main Canadian cities, especially the city of Montreal, have to face a serious problem on account of the cost of living index which is constantly rising, especially since this government has assumed office. It must be borne in mind that from an economic point of view an emergency situation prevails in Montreal. It has 55,000 unemployed and 25 per cent of its workers do not earn enough to provide an adequate standard of living for their families.
How can heads of families in cities such as Montreal overcome their difficulties if the cost of living keeps on rising? And the same situation is true in every Canadian city.
I would be very happy to know what the Minister of Finance intends to do to stabilize the cost of living and check further increases because there will come a time when the situation will become unbearable for the Canadian worker. I should like to know what the government intends to do to remedy such a catastrophic situation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can quite understand the hon. member raising
[Mr. Favreau.l

this very important question of the rising cost of living index. I notice that he brought to our attention the fact that the largest increase had occurred in the city of Montreal. Of course I should point out to him that this situation fluctuates from city to city, so that while in the period of May and June the city of Montreal may have been the city that had the largest increase, it does not necessarily follow, of course, that the cost of living index will be constantly rising at a higher rate in the city of Montreal than elsewhere.
The movement of consumer prices in Canada over the past year has been moderate and in line with the experience of the past few years. Over the past year, prices have risen about 2 per cent, about the same rate of increase that was experienced during the previous three or four years. Not all kinds of prices have risen at this rate. Services, particularly medical costs and automobile insurance, have risen more-by some 2.4 per cent. Prices of durable goods, such as appliances, are actually lower now than they were a year ago.
It is worth noting that the rise in prices in Canada has been only fractionally higher than it was in the United States. It is well below the price rises which have been occurring in most European countries and Japan. I noted that the hon. member quoted the Financial Times, I believe, as a source of his information, and I am sure he will agree that it is only proper that I should reply in kind. Only last week-that is, on July 13- the Financial Times of Canada had this to say:
Routine monthly reporting of changes in Canada's consumer price index repeatedly brings newspaper headlines of "new record highs". But it does not follow that the cost of living is skyrocketing every time the index moves up-
The longer-range trend of consumer prices remains remarkably stable. The June index was 1.9 per cent above June, 1963, but the increase in ten months since August has been only 1 per cent.
This is well in line with the average annual increase of 2 per cent experienced in recent years. It is also significant that industrial wages and salaries have been increasing at a steadily faster rate than consumer prices. The industrial wage index stood at 200.8 at May 1, (1949=100), compared with 198.5 a month earlier and 194.4 a year earlier.
The total wage index has thus risen 100 per cent since 1949, for an average annual gain of 6.6 per

cent while the consumer price index has increased only 35 per cent, or just over 2 per cent per year.
